name: Data Structures and Algorithms
audience: Developers preparing for technical interviews or wanting a solid algorithms foundation, using Python. Basic Python assumed.
format: This site's course with a 40-question practice test of complexity analysis, trace-the-algorithm, choose-the-structure and debugging questions.

domains.name: Complexity and algorithmic thinking
domains.summary: Big-O, Theta and Omega, best, worst and average cases, and amortized analysis of dynamic arrays. Also covers recurrences and the master theorem, correctness arguments with loop invariants and induction, and the real cost of Python's built-in list, dict, set, deque and string operations.

domains.name: Arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues and hashing
domains.summary: Dynamic arrays versus linked lists, stacks, queues, deques and monotonic stacks, and how hash tables handle collisions, load factor and resizing. Also covers two pointers, sliding windows, prefix sums and hash-based designs such as frequency counts and an LRU cache.

domains.name: Trees, heaps and advanced structures
domains.summary: Tree traversals and recursion on trees, binary search trees and balanced trees at a conceptual level, and heaps with heapq for top-k and k-way merge. Also covers tries, union-find with path compression, and segment and Fenwick trees for range queries.

domains.name: Sorting, searching and divide and conquer
domains.summary: Merge sort, quicksort and heapsort, stability and the comparison-sort lower bound, counting and radix sort, and Python's built-in sort with key functions. Also covers binary search invariants with bisect, searching on the answer, quickselect, and choosing the right sort or search for the data.

domains.name: Graphs
domains.summary: Adjacency lists versus matrices and modelling problems as graphs, BFS and DFS, cycle detection and topological sort for dependency resolution. Also covers Dijkstra and Bellman-Ford for weighted shortest paths, minimum spanning trees and strongly connected components.

domains.name: Dynamic programming, greedy and problem solving
domains.summary: Designing DP states with memoization or tabulation, classic DP problems such as knapsack, LIS and edit distance, and greedy algorithms proved by exchange arguments. Also covers backtracking with pruning, a method for interview problems, and P, NP and NP-completeness at a working level.

scenarios.title: A coding interview at a large tech company
scenarios.description: You have 45 minutes and a whiteboard-style problem. Clarify the constraints, pick a structure and an algorithm that fit them, state the complexity, and test the edge cases before you finish.

scenarios.title: Choosing a data structure for a cache
scenarios.description: A service needs a bounded in-memory cache with fast lookups and eviction. Weigh dicts, OrderedDict, heaps and linked lists against the access pattern and the eviction policy.

scenarios.title: Routing and dependency resolution
scenarios.description: Model roads, networks or package dependencies as graphs. Pick BFS, Dijkstra or Bellman-Ford for routes, and topological sort to order builds and detect cycles.

scenarios.title: Ranking and top-k over a stream
scenarios.description: Events arrive faster than you can sort them. Keep the top k items, running medians or merged sorted feeds with heaps and bounded memory.

scenarios.title: Optimizing an O(n²) hot path
scenarios.description: A profiler points at a nested loop. Replace it with hashing, sorting with two pointers, prefix sums or a better data structure, and confirm the gain holds on real input sizes.

lessons.title: Asymptotic notation and the cases of analysis
lessons.summary: How Big-O, Omega and Theta bound the growth of a function, why they are not the same thing as worst, best and average case, and how to count the work of loops.

sections.heading: Why count growth instead of seconds
sections.body:
Wall-clock time depends on the machine, the interpreter and the input. Asymptotic analysis asks a narrower question: as the input size $$n$$ grows, how fast does the number of basic steps grow? Constants and lower-order terms are dropped because, for large enough $$n$$, the leading term dominates.

That does not mean constants never matter. Two $$\Theta(n\log n)$$ sorts can differ by a factor of several in practice. Asymptotics tells you which algorithm wins *eventually*, and which one will collapse when the input grows 100 times.

sections.heading: Big-O, Omega and Theta
sections.body:
Let $$f$$ and $$g$$ be functions of $$n$$.

| Notation | Meaning | Informal reading |
|---|---|---|
| $$f(n)=O(g(n))$$ | there exist $$c>0, n_0$$ with $$f(n)\le c\,g(n)$$ for all $$n\ge n_0$$ | grows **no faster** than $$g$$ |
| $$f(n)=\Omega(g(n))$$ | there exist $$c>0, n_0$$ with $$f(n)\ge c\,g(n)$$ for all $$n\ge n_0$$ | grows **at least** as fast as $$g$$ |
| $$f(n)=\Theta(g(n))$$ | both of the above | grows **at the same rate** as $$g$$ |

Example: $$f(n)=3n^2+100n\log n$$ is $$\Theta(n^2)$$. It is also $$O(n^3)$$ (a true but loose upper bound) and $$\Omega(n)$$ (a true but loose lower bound). It is **not** $$O(n\log n)$$.

When people say "this is $$O(n^2)$$" they usually mean the tight bound $$\Theta(n^2)$$. On an exam, read the notation literally.

sections.heading: Notation is not the same as case
sections.body:
Worst, best and average case are choices about **which input** you analyse. Big-O, Omega and Theta are statements about **a function**. The two are independent:

- Insertion sort's worst-case running time is $$\Theta(n^2)$$ (reverse-sorted input). Its best case is $$\Theta(n)$$ (already sorted input).
- Quicksort with a fixed first-element pivot has a worst case of about $$n^2/2$$ compares, on already sorted input. Its average over random orderings is about $$2n\ln n\approx1.39\,n\lg n$$ compares. Shuffling the input first makes the bad case vanishingly unlikely.

So "Big-O means worst case" is a common misconception. You can give a Theta bound on the best case, or an O bound on the average case.

sections.heading: Counting loops
sections.body:
Most analysis reduces to summing the work of loops.

```python
for i in range(n):          # n iterations
    for j in range(i, n):   # n - i iterations
        work()              # O(1)
```

Total: $$\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(n-i)=n(n+1)/2=\Theta(n^2)$$.

A doubling loop behaves differently:

```python
i = 1
while i < n:
    for j in range(i):      # i iterations
        work()
    i *= 2
```

The inner counts are $$1+2+4+\dots<2n$$, a geometric series, so the total is $$\Theta(n)$$ even though there are two nested loops. Nesting depth alone does not tell you the cost; sum what actually runs.

Common orders, slowest growing first: $$1 < \log n < n < n\log n < n^2 < n^3 < 2^n < n!$$.

keyPoints: O is an upper bound, Omega a lower bound, Theta both; each holds for all n beyond some n0, up to a constant factor.
Worst, best and average case pick the input; O, Omega and Theta describe the resulting function. They are independent choices.
Drop constants and lower-order terms, but remember that constants still matter between algorithms of the same order.
Sum the actual iterations: a doubling outer loop with an inner loop of i steps is Theta(n), not Theta(n log n).

gotchas.trap: Big-O means worst case and Omega means best case.
gotchas.correct: Big-O and Omega are bounds on a function. You can state any of them for the worst, best or average case.

gotchas.trap: Two nested loops are always Theta(n^2).
gotchas.correct: Add up the iterations that really run. Geometric inner loops sum to Theta(n), and inner loops of log n steps give Theta(n log n).

gotchas.trap: If f is O(n^3), it cannot also be O(n^2).
gotchas.correct: O is only an upper bound, so a Theta(n^2) function is O(n^2), O(n^3) and O(2^n). Give the tightest bound you can justify.

lessons.lab: Write a function that counts how many times `work()` runs for each loop pattern in this lesson, for n = 1,000 to 1,000,000 by factors of 10. Plot or print count / n and count / n**2, and check that the ratio which stays roughly constant matches the Theta bound you derived.

lessons.title: Amortized analysis and Python's cost model
lessons.summary: Why list.append is O(1) amortized, the aggregate, accounting and potential arguments that prove it, and the operation costs of list, dict, set, deque and str that decide whether your Python code is linear or quadratic.

sections.heading: Amortized cost
sections.body:
An amortized bound is a **worst-case guarantee over any sequence of operations**: $$m$$ operations take at most $$m$$ times the amortized cost in total. A single operation may be expensive, but the expensive ones are rare enough that the average **per operation** over the sequence stays low.

This is not average-case analysis. There is no probability and no assumption about random input. It is a bound on the total cost of the worst possible sequence.

sections.heading: Dynamic arrays and geometric growth
sections.body:
A dynamic array keeps spare capacity. Appending is cheap until the array is full; then it allocates a larger block and copies every element.

- If capacity grows by a **constant factor** $$r>1$$, the copy sizes form a geometric series. For $$n$$ appends the total copying is $$O(n)$$, so each append is $$O(1)$$ amortized.
- If capacity grows by a **fixed amount** $$k$$, resizes happen every $$k$$ appends and copy $$k, 2k, 3k, \dots$$ elements. The total is about $$n^2/(2k)=\Theta(n^2)$$, so each append is $$\Theta(n)$$ amortized.

CPython's list grows by roughly 1.125 times plus a small constant, not by doubling. Any factor above 1 gives $$O(1)$$ amortized append, so the exact factor is an implementation detail. Do not rely on specific capacities or byte sizes.

sections.heading: Aggregate, accounting and potential
sections.body:
Three standard ways to prove an amortized bound:

1. **Aggregate.** Bound the total cost of any $$n$$ operations, then divide by $$n$$. For doubling arrays: $$n$$ writes plus copies of $$1+2+4+\dots<2n$$, total under $$3n$$.
2. **Accounting (banker's).** Charge each operation a fixed fee, say 3 units for an append. One pays for the write and the rest is saved as credit on the data structure. When a resize happens, the saved credit pays for the copies. The proof obligation is that the credit never goes negative.
3. **Potential.** Define a function $$\Phi$$ of the structure's state with $$\Phi\ge0$$ and $$\Phi_0=0$$. Amortized cost = actual cost + $$\Delta\Phi$$. Cheap operations raise $$\Phi$$, and expensive ones spend it.

sections.heading: Python's cost model
sections.body:
From the official time-complexity table (CPython, exact built-in types):

| Operation | Cost |
|---|---|
| `l.append(x)` | $$O(1)$$ amortized |
| `l[i]`, `l[i] = x`, `len(l)` | $$O(1)$$ |
| `l.pop()` | $$O(1)$$ |
| `l.pop(k)`, `l.insert(k, x)` | $$O(n-k)$$; index 0 is the worst case |
| `x in l` | $$O(n)$$ |
| `l[i:j]` | $$O(j-i)$$ (it copies) |
| `l.sort()` | $$O(n\log n)$$; adaptive, $$O(n)$$ comparisons on sorted or reverse-sorted input |
| `x in s`, `s.add`, `s.discard` | $$O(1)$$ average |
| `s1 & s2` | $$O(\min(\lvert s_1\rvert,\lvert s_2\rvert))$$ |
| `s1 \| s2` | $$O(\lvert s_1\rvert+\lvert s_2\rvert)$$ |
| `k in d`, `d[k]`, `d[k] = v`, `del d[k]` | $$O(1)$$ average |
| `s + t` (str) | $$O(\lvert s\rvert+\lvert t\rvert)$$ |

The dict and set figures are **average** case and assume hashing and comparing a key is $$O(1)$$. If every key hashes to the same value, each of those operations degrades to $$O(n)$$. Removing many entries does not shrink the table, so iterating or copying a dict after mass deletion still costs time proportional to its former size until a later insertion resizes it.

The table has no deque entry. The `collections` docs say a deque supports appends and pops from either end in approximately $$O(1)$$, while indexing slows to $$O(n)$$ in the middle.

sections.heading: Patterns that turn linear into quadratic
sections.body:
```python
# Quadratic: pop(0) shifts every remaining element
while queue:
    item = queue.pop(0)

# Linear: deque pops from the left in O(1)
from collections import deque
q = deque(queue)
while q:
    item = q.popleft()
```

Other repeat offenders:

- `x in some_list` inside a loop over $$m$$ items costs $$O(nm)$$. Build `set(some_list)` once for $$O(n+m)$$ average.
- `out += piece` on a `str` in a loop: the docs warn that building a string by concatenating many pieces in a loop is quadratic in the total length. Collect the pieces in a list and call `''.join(pieces)` once.
- Slicing inside recursion (`helper(a[mid:])`) copies the slice every call. Pass indices instead.

keyPoints: Amortized cost bounds the total over any sequence of operations; it involves no probability.
Constant-factor growth gives O(1) amortized append; fixed-increment growth gives Theta(n) amortized append.
CPython lists over-allocate by about 1.125x, not 2x; the factor is an implementation detail.
list.pop(0) and insert(0, x) are O(n); use collections.deque for queues.
dict and set operations are O(1) on average and O(n) in the worst case when keys collide.
Build strings with ''.join, not repeated +=, and test membership against a set, not a list.

gotchas.trap: Amortized O(1) means every append is O(1).
gotchas.correct: An individual append may be O(n) when the list resizes. Only the cost averaged over the sequence is O(1).

gotchas.trap: CPython doubles a list's capacity when it fills up.
gotchas.correct: CPython grows lists by roughly 1.125x plus a constant. What matters for the amortized bound is that the factor is greater than 1.

gotchas.trap: dict lookups are always O(1).
gotchas.correct: They are O(1) on average. If many keys share a hash value, lookups degrade toward O(n).

gotchas.trap: A deque is a list with faster ends, so d[i] is O(1) everywhere.
gotchas.correct: Deque indexing is O(1) at the ends but O(n) in the middle. Use a list for random access.

lessons.lab: Time three ways of draining a 100,000-item queue: `list.pop(0)`, `deque.popleft()`, and reversing once then using `list.pop()`. Then time building a 1,000,000-character string with `+=` versus `''.join`. Use `time.perf_counter` and double n a few times to see which approaches scale linearly.

lessons.title: Recursion, recurrences and correctness
lessons.summary: Turning recursive code into a recurrence, solving it with a recursion tree or the master theorem, and proving code correct with induction and loop invariants before choosing the edge cases to test.

sections.heading: From recursive code to a recurrence
sections.body:
A recurrence describes the cost of a recursive function in terms of the cost of its subcalls.

- Merge sort makes two calls on halves and merges in linear time: $$T(n)=2T(n/2)+\Theta(n)$$.
- Binary search makes one call on a half and does constant work: $$T(n)=T(n/2)+\Theta(1)$$.
- A function that peels off one element and does linear work: $$T(n)=T(n-1)+\Theta(n)$$.

Count the number of subcalls ($$a$$), how much smaller each one is ($$n/b$$ or $$n-1$$), and the non-recursive work $$f(n)$$, including hidden costs such as slicing.

sections.heading: Recursion trees
sections.body:
Draw the calls as a tree and add up the work level by level.

For $$T(n)=2T(n/2)+n$$: level $$i$$ has $$2^i$$ nodes, each doing $$n/2^i$$ work, so every level costs $$n$$. There are about $$\log_2 n$$ levels, total $$\Theta(n\log n)$$.

For $$T(n)=T(n-1)+n$$: the levels cost $$n, n-1, \dots, 1$$, total $$n(n+1)/2=\Theta(n^2)$$.

The tree tells you where the work lives: evenly spread (each level equal), concentrated at the root (levels shrink geometrically) or at the leaves (levels grow geometrically).

sections.heading: The master theorem
sections.body:
For $$T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n)$$ with $$a\ge1$$, $$b>1$$, compare $$f(n)$$ with $$n^{\log_b a}$$, the total work at the leaves:

| Case | Condition | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1, leaves dominate | $$f(n)=O(n^{\log_b a-\varepsilon})$$ for some $$\varepsilon>0$$ | $$T(n)=\Theta(n^{\log_b a})$$ |
| 2, balanced | $$f(n)=\Theta(n^{\log_b a})$$ | $$T(n)=\Theta(n^{\log_b a}\log n)$$ |
| 3, root dominates | $$f(n)=\Omega(n^{\log_b a+\varepsilon})$$ and $$a\,f(n/b)\le c\,f(n)$$ for some $$c<1$$ | $$T(n)=\Theta(f(n))$$ |

Examples: $$2T(n/2)+n$$ is case 2, giving $$\Theta(n\log n)$$. $$8T(n/2)+n^2$$ has $$n^{\log_2 8}=n^3$$, case 1, giving $$\Theta(n^3)$$. $$2T(n/2)+n^2$$ is case 3, giving $$\Theta(n^2)$$. $$T(n/2)+1$$ is case 2 with $$n^0=1$$, giving $$\Theta(\log n)$$.

The theorem does not apply to subtract-and-conquer recurrences such as $$T(n-1)+n$$. Use a recursion tree or substitution.

sections.heading: Recursion depth in Python
sections.body:
CPython does not optimise tail calls, and the default recursion limit returned by `sys.getrecursionlimit()` is 1000. A recursive DFS on a path-shaped graph with 10,000 nodes, or memoised recursion that recurses $$n$$ deep for large $$n$$, raises `RecursionError`.

Options: rewrite with an explicit stack (usually best), restructure so depth is $$O(\log n)$$, or raise the limit with `sys.setrecursionlimit`. The `sys` docs warn that the highest possible limit is platform-dependent and that a too-high limit can lead to a crash, so prefer the iterative rewrite for inputs of unknown depth.

sections.heading: Correctness: induction and loop invariants
sections.body:
**Induction** proves recursive code: show the base cases are right, then show that if every call on a *strictly smaller* input is correct, the current call is correct. If a subcall is not strictly smaller, the proof fails, and so does the code, often with infinite recursion:

```python
def total(a):
    if not a:
        return 0
    mid = len(a) // 2
    return total(a[:mid]) + total(a[mid:])  # len 1: mid = 0, a[0:] is a again
```

Adding `if len(a) == 1: return a[0]` restores progress.

A **loop invariant** proves iterative code. It is a statement that is true:

1. **Initialization:** before the first iteration.
2. **Maintenance:** if true before an iteration, still true after it.
3. **Termination:** when the loop ends, the invariant plus the exit condition give the result you want.

For `best = a[0]; for i in range(1, n): best = max(best, a[i])`, the invariant is "at the start of iteration i, `best == max(a[:i])`". At exit $$i=n$$, so `best` is the maximum.

sections.heading: Choosing edge cases
sections.body:
Invariants and recurrences tell you where code breaks. Test those boundaries on purpose:

- Empty input and a single element.
- Targets before the first element, after the last, and exactly at both ends.
- Duplicates, especially for search and partitioning.
- All-equal and already sorted or reverse-sorted input, which trigger worst cases in naive quicksort.
- Sizes that make recursion deep, and values at numeric limits.

Compare the function with a slow, obviously correct reference on many small random inputs. That catches off-by-one errors that a few large hand-picked tests miss.

keyPoints: Write a recurrence by counting subcalls, their sizes and the non-recursive work, including slicing.
Recursion trees show where work concentrates: root, levels or leaves.
Master theorem: compare f(n) with n^(log_b a); smaller means leaves dominate, equal adds a log factor, larger means f(n) dominates.
The master theorem does not cover T(n) = T(n-1) + f(n).
CPython's default recursion limit is 1000 and there is no tail-call optimisation; use an explicit stack for deep inputs.
A loop invariant needs initialization, maintenance and a useful termination step; induction needs strictly smaller subproblems.

gotchas.trap: T(n) = T(n-1) + n can be solved with the master theorem.
gotchas.correct: The master theorem needs subproblems of size n/b. Sum the recursion tree: the result is Theta(n^2).

gotchas.trap: Recursive binary search on a[mid:] is O(log n).
gotchas.correct: Each slice copies up to n/2 elements, so the total is Theta(n). Pass lo and hi indices to get Theta(log n).

gotchas.trap: Python optimises tail-recursive functions, so deep tail recursion is safe.
gotchas.correct: CPython does no tail-call elimination; every call uses a frame and counts toward the recursion limit.

gotchas.trap: An invariant that holds at every step is enough.
gotchas.correct: It must also yield the desired result at termination. 'best is an element of a' holds throughout but proves nothing about the maximum.

lessons.title: Dynamic arrays and linked lists
lessons.summary: The two ways to store a sequence: contiguous memory with geometric growth, or nodes joined by pointers. Which operations each makes cheap, and why Python code almost always starts from a list.

sections.heading: The sequence interface
sections.body:
A **sequence** keeps items in an order you choose and supports operations such as get or set at index i, insert or delete at index i, and insert or delete at either end. MIT 6.006 separates the *interface* (what operations exist) from the *data structure* (how they are implemented and what each costs). The same interface can be implemented in very different ways:

| Operation | Static array | Dynamic array (Python `list`) | Singly linked list | Doubly linked list (with tail) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| get / set at i | O(1) | O(1) | O(i) | O(min(i, n-i)) |
| insert / delete at end | O(n) (copy) | O(1) amortized | O(n) delete, O(1) insert with tail pointer | O(1) |
| insert / delete at front | O(n) | O(n) | O(1) | O(1) |
| insert / delete next to a node you already hold | O(n) | O(n) | O(1) after it | O(1) before or after |

The last row is the one that makes linked lists worth knowing.

sections.heading: Dynamic arrays and amortized append
sections.body:
A dynamic array stores items contiguously in a buffer with **spare capacity**. Appending writes into the next free slot in O(1). When the buffer is full, it allocates a larger buffer and copies everything, which costs O(n) for that one append.

The trick is to grow **geometrically**: multiply the capacity by a constant factor greater than 1. Then the total copying over n appends is a geometric series bounded by a constant times n, so each append is O(1) **amortized**. Growing by a fixed number of slots (say +10 each time) gives total copying of order $$n^2/10$$, which is O(n) per append.

CPython's list over-allocates by roughly an eighth plus a small constant, not by doubling. The exact factor is an implementation detail. What matters is that it is geometric. The official cost table lists `append` as O(1) amortized, with the note that an individual append may occasionally be O(n) when the storage is resized.

Inserting or deleting at index k shifts every later element: `insert(k, x)`, `pop(k)` and `del a[k]` are O(n-k). Index 0 is the worst case, the end is O(1).

sections.heading: Linked lists
sections.body:
A **linked list** stores each item in a node that points to the next node (and, in a doubly linked list, to the previous one). Nodes can live anywhere in memory, so:

- Inserting or removing next to a node you already hold is O(1): rewire a few pointers, move nothing.
- Reaching index i means walking i pointers, so random access is O(i).
- A **singly** linked list cannot delete its tail in O(1), even with a tail pointer, because finding the new tail needs the predecessor. A **doubly** linked list fixes that.
- Every node carries pointer overhead and the nodes are scattered, so traversal has poor cache locality compared with a contiguous array.

Sentinel (dummy) head and tail nodes remove the "is this the first or last node?" special cases from insert and delete code.

sections.heading: When each wins in practice
sections.body:
- **Default to a list** for indexed access, appends, iteration and sorting. Contiguous storage is fast and the API is rich.
- **Use `collections.deque`** when you push or pop at *both* ends. It gives O(1) operations at either end, while a list pays O(n) for `pop(0)` and `insert(0, v)`.
- **Use a hand-built doubly linked list** when you must splice or remove items in the *middle* in O(1) and you already hold a reference to the node, typically because a hash map points at it (the LRU cache design).
- If you mostly need index access in the middle, neither a linked list nor a deque helps: the collections docs note that deque indexing is O(1) at both ends but slows to O(n) in the middle.

keyPoints: Geometric growth (any factor > 1) makes append O(1) amortized; fixed-increment growth makes it O(n).
list insert/pop/del at index k cost O(n-k); the front is the worst case.
Linked lists win only for O(1) splicing at a node you already hold; random access is O(i).
A singly linked list cannot delete its tail in O(1); a doubly linked list can.
Use deque, not list, for work at both ends.

gotchas.trap: CPython lists double their capacity when full.
gotchas.correct: CPython over-allocates by roughly 1.125x plus a constant. Any geometric factor gives amortized O(1) append; the exact factor is an implementation detail.

gotchas.trap: A linked list makes insertion at position i O(1).
gotchas.correct: Only once you hold the node. Finding position i first costs O(i).

gotchas.trap: Amortized O(1) means every append is fast.
gotchas.correct: Individual appends that trigger a resize cost O(n); the bound is on the average over a sequence.

lessons.title: Stacks, queues, deques and monotonic structures
lessons.summary: LIFO and FIFO containers, how to get O(1) operations from Python, and the monotonic stack and queue patterns that turn quadratic scans into linear ones.

sections.heading: Stacks: last in, first out
Queues and deques
sections.body:
A **queue** is first in, first out: enqueue at the back, dequeue from the front. A list is a poor queue because `pop(0)` shifts every remaining element, O(n). Use `collections.deque`: `append` and `popleft` are O(1), and the docs describe "approximately the same O(1) performance in either direction".

A **deque** (double-ended queue) supports O(1) push and pop at both ends. Useful extras:

- `deque(maxlen=k)` is a bounded buffer: when full, adding at one end discards from the other. `deque(maxlen=3)` extended with `[1, 2, 3, 4]` holds `[2, 3, 4]`. Calling `insert` on a full bounded deque raises IndexError.
- `rotate(n)` rotates right by n; `rotate(1)` equals `appendleft(pop())`.
- Indexing is O(1) near the ends but O(n) in the middle, so a deque is not a random-access array.

BFS on a graph is the canonical queue user.

sections.heading: Monotonic stacks
sections.body:
A **monotonic stack** keeps its contents in sorted order (for example, decreasing values from bottom to top). When a new element arrives, pop everything it "beats", then push it. Each popped element has just found its answer.

**Next greater element:** for each position, the first later value that is larger.

```python
def next_greater(a):
    res = [-1] * len(a)
    stack = []                      # indices; their values are non-increasing
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        while stack and a[stack[-1]] < x:
            res[stack.pop()] = x
        stack.append(i)
    return res

next_greater([2, 1, 2, 4, 3])       # [4, 2, 4, -1, -1]
```

Every index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the whole loop is O(n) even though it contains a nested `while`. The same shape solves "days until a warmer temperature", the largest rectangle in a histogram and stock-span problems.

sections.heading: Monotonic queues and sliding window maximum
sections.body:
A **monotonic deque** answers "max (or min) of the last k items" in O(1) per step. Store indices whose values are decreasing from front to back:

```python
from collections import deque

def window_max(a, k):
    q, out = deque(), []
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        while q and a[q[-1]] <= x:   # smaller items can never be the max again
            q.pop()
        q.append(i)
        if q[0] <= i - k:            # front fell out of the window
            q.popleft()
        if i >= k - 1:
            out.append(a[q[0]])
    return out

window_max([1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7], 3)   # [3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7]
```

Total work is O(n): each index enters and leaves the deque at most once. The naive version that calls `max` on every window is O(nk). A heap also works in O(n log n) but needs lazy removal of expired entries.

keyPoints: list is a fine stack: append/pop at the end are O(1).
Use deque.popleft for queues; list.pop(0) is O(n).
deque(maxlen=k) keeps the last k items automatically.
Monotonic stacks and deques are O(n) overall because each element is pushed and popped at most once.
deque indexing is O(n) in the middle; it is not a random-access array.

gotchas.trap: A nested while loop inside a for loop means O(n^2).
gotchas.correct: Count total pushes and pops. In a monotonic stack each element is popped at most once, so the total is O(n).

gotchas.trap: queue.Queue is the fast queue for single-threaded BFS.
gotchas.correct: queue.Queue adds locking for threads. For an algorithmic queue in one thread, use collections.deque.

gotchas.trap: Checking only that every closer matches its opener validates brackets.
gotchas.correct: You must also reject a closer on an empty stack and any leftover openers at the end.

Check that `[73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73]` gives `[1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0]`. Then implement `window_min` by flipping one comparison in `window_max` and test it against a brute-force version on random inputs.

lessons.title: Hash tables: collisions, load factor and resizing
lessons.summary: How a hash table turns a key into an array index, the two families of collision handling, why load factor controls speed, and what Python requires of a key.

sections.heading: From keys to buckets
sections.body:
A hash table stores key-value pairs in an array of M slots. A **hash function** maps each key to an integer, reduced to an index in `[0, M)`. If the hash spreads keys evenly, lookups, inserts and deletes take expected O(1) time.

Two keys landing in the same slot is a **collision**. Collisions are unavoidable once there are more possible keys than slots, so every hash table needs a collision strategy. MIT 6.006 introduces hashing as a way to beat the comparison-model lower bound for search, and 6.046 covers **universal hashing**: choosing the hash function at random from a family so that no fixed input is bad for every choice, giving expected O(1) operations regardless of the keys.

sections.heading: Separate chaining
sections.body:
**Separate chaining** keeps a small list (chain) in each slot. Insert hashes to a slot and adds to that chain; search scans one chain.

With N keys and M chains, the average chain length is the **load factor** $$\alpha = N/M$$. Princeton's *Algorithms* states that, under the uniform hashing assumption, the number of compares for search and insert is proportional to N/M. Chaining tolerates $$\alpha > 1$$, but if M stays fixed while N grows, operations degrade towards linear time. The fix is to **resize**: when $$\alpha$$ passes a threshold, allocate a larger array (typically about double) and rehash every key, which keeps $$\alpha$$ bounded and the amortized cost per operation constant.

sections.heading: Open addressing and linear probing
sections.body:
**Open addressing** stores keys directly in the array. On a collision it probes other slots in a fixed sequence. **Linear probing** tries i, i+1, i+2, ... (wrapping around) until it finds the key or an empty slot.

Here $$\alpha$$ must stay below 1, and performance falls sharply as it approaches 1 because occupied slots form long **clusters**. Under the uniform hashing assumption, algs4 gives the expected probes as about

$$\tfrac12\left(1+\tfrac{1}{1-\alpha}\right)$$ for a search hit and $$\tfrac12\left(1+\tfrac{1}{(1-\alpha)^2}\right)$$ for a miss or insert.

At $$\alpha = 1/2$$ that is about 1.5 and 2.5 probes; at $$\alpha = 0.9$$ a miss averages about 50. That is why linear-probing tables resize to keep $$\alpha$$ at or below about one half.

**Deletion is subtle:** simply emptying a slot can break the probe sequence of keys inserted after it, so later searches stop early and miss them. algs4 reinserts the rest of the cluster after a delete; other designs leave a "deleted" marker (tombstone).

sections.heading: What Python requires of a key
sections.body:
Python's `dict` and `set` are hash tables. Their contract, from the data model docs: objects that compare equal **must** have the same hash, and a key's hash must not change while it is in a table.

- Built-in mutable containers (`list`, `dict`, `set`) are unhashable; use `tuple` or `frozenset` as keys.
- A class that defines `__eq__` without `__hash__` has its `__hash__` set to None and becomes unhashable. Define `__hash__` from the same fields `__eq__` uses, and keep those fields immutable (a frozen dataclass does this for you).
- `1`, `1.0` and `True` compare equal and hash equal, so they are the same dict key.
- String hashes are randomized per process (unless PYTHONHASHSEED is set), which defends against crafted collisions. Never persist hash values or rely on the iteration order of a set of strings.

The official cost table lists dict and set operations as O(1) **average**. In the worst case, when every key hashes to the same value, each becomes O(n). The same table notes that dicts do not shrink when items are removed.

keyPoints: Load factor α = N/M drives cost; resize (about double M and rehash) to keep it bounded.
Chaining: average cost proportional to N/M. Linear probing: α < 1 required, and probes explode as α nears 1.
Deleting from a linear-probing table needs cluster reinsertion or tombstones.
Equal objects must have equal hashes; mutable built-ins are unhashable.
dict/set O(1) is average case; all-colliding keys make operations O(n).

gotchas.trap: Hash table operations are O(1) worst case.
gotchas.correct: They are O(1) expected or average. Adversarial or degenerate hashing makes each O(n).

gotchas.trap: Defining __eq__ on a class keeps it usable as a dict key.
gotchas.correct: Defining __eq__ without __hash__ makes instances unhashable. Define a consistent __hash__.

gotchas.trap: Deleting from an open-addressing table just clears the slot.
gotchas.correct: That breaks probe chains. Reinsert the following cluster or mark a tombstone.

Instrument `get` to count probes, insert 10,000 random integers with resizing switched off and on, and compare the average probes for misses against the formula in this lesson. Then deliberately break `delete` (just clear the slot) and write a test that shows a key becoming unfindable.

lessons.title: Array techniques: two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums
lessons.summary: Four linear-time patterns that replace nested loops over arrays: two pointers on sorted data, variable and fixed sliding windows, prefix sums for range queries, and difference arrays for range updates.

sections.heading: Two pointers
sections.body:
On a **sorted** array, two indices moving toward each other can find a pair with a target sum in O(n):

```python
def pair_with_sum(a, target):        # a is sorted ascending
    i, j = 0, len(a) - 1
    while i < j:
        s = a[i] + a[j]
        if s == target:
            return i, j
        if s < target:
            i += 1                   # need a bigger sum
        else:
            j -= 1                   # need a smaller sum
    return None
```

Why it is safe to discard: if `a[i] + a[j] < target`, then `a[i]` plus any element left of j is even smaller, so `a[i]` cannot be in any pair and i can advance. The argument depends on sorted order. On unsorted data, either sort first (O(n log n)) or use a hash set of seen values (O(n) expected). Other two-pointer shapes include a slow and a fast pointer for in-place compaction (removing duplicates from a sorted array) and merging two sorted arrays.

sections.heading: Sliding window
sections.body:
A **window** is a contiguous range `[lo, i]` that moves right. Each element enters once and leaves once, so the scan is O(n).

- **Fixed size k:** add the new element, remove the one that fell out (running sum, counts, or a monotonic deque for max/min).
- **Variable size:** grow the right edge; while the window breaks a condition, shrink from the left.

Longest substring without repeated characters:

```python
def longest_unique(s):
    last, lo, best = {}, 0, 0
    for i, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in last and last[ch] >= lo:   # repeat inside the window
            lo = last[ch] + 1
        last[ch] = i
        best = max(best, i - lo + 1)
    return best

longest_unique("abcabcbb"), longest_unique("abba")   # (3, 2)
```

Dropping the `last[ch] >= lo` check moves `lo` backwards on inputs like `"abba"` and returns 3 instead of 2.

Shrinking windows rely on **monotonicity**: extending the window must never make a violated condition true again, and shrinking must never make it false. Sums of non-negative numbers have this property; sums that can include negatives do not.

sections.heading: Prefix sums
sections.body:
A **prefix sum** array `P` has `P[0] = 0` and `P[i+1] = P[i] + a[i]`. Then the sum of `a[l:r]` is `P[r] - P[l]`, O(1) per query after O(n) setup. `itertools.accumulate(a, initial=0)` builds it: `[3, 1, 4, 1, 5]` gives `[0, 3, 4, 8, 9, 14]`.

Prefix sums combine with hashing to count subarrays with sum k, **including negative numbers**, where sliding windows fail. A subarray ending at i sums to k exactly when some earlier prefix equals `P - k`:

```python
from collections import Counter

def count_subarrays(a, k):
    seen = Counter({0: 1})       # the empty prefix
    total = prefix = 0
    for x in a:
        prefix += x
        total += seen[prefix - k]
        seen[prefix] += 1
    return total

count_subarrays([1, 2, 3, -3, 3], 3)   # 5
```

The 2-D version (summed-area table) answers rectangle-sum queries in O(1).

sections.heading: Difference arrays
sections.body:
A **difference array** is the inverse trick: it makes **range updates** O(1). To add v to every element of `a[l..r]` (inclusive), do `D[l] += v` and `D[r+1] -= v` on an array one longer than `a`. After all updates, a single prefix-sum pass recovers the values.

```python
from itertools import accumulate
n = 5
D = [0] * (n + 1)
for l, r, v in [(1, 3, 2), (0, 1, 5), (2, 4, 1)]:
    D[l] += v
    D[r + 1] -= v
list(accumulate(D[:n]))        # [5, 7, 3, 3, 1]
```

q updates and one read cost O(n + q) instead of O(nq). Use it for booking or flight-reservation counts, interval coverage and "how many intervals contain each point". If updates and queries interleave many times, a Fenwick or segment tree (covered in the trees domain) is the better tool.

keyPoints: Two pointers on sorted data find pairs in O(n); the correctness argument needs sorted order.
Sliding windows are O(n) because each element enters and leaves once; shrinking needs a monotone condition.
Prefix sums give O(1) range sums: sum(a[l:r]) = P[r] - P[l].
Prefix sum plus a hash of counts handles subarray-sum problems with negative numbers.
Difference arrays make range updates O(1), then one prefix pass reads all values.

gotchas.trap: A sliding window finds subarrays with sum k for any integers.
gotchas.correct: Only for non-negative values. With negatives, use prefix sums with a hash map of counts.

gotchas.trap: Prefix sums without a leading 0 are fine.
gotchas.correct: Starting P with 0 avoids off-by-one special cases for ranges that begin at index 0.

gotchas.trap: In a difference array, the decrement goes at index r.
gotchas.correct: For an inclusive range [l, r], decrement at r + 1 (allocate n + 1 slots).

lessons.lab: Write `min_window_len(a, target)`: the length of the shortest contiguous subarray of non-negative integers with sum at least target (0 if none), using a shrinking window. Test it against an O(n^2) brute force on 1,000 random arrays. Then show, with a concrete array containing a negative number, why the window version gives a wrong answer, and solve the "sum exactly k" variant with prefix sums and a Counter.

lessons.title: Designing with hashing: counts, dedup and LRU caches
lessons.summary: Using dicts, sets and the collections module as building blocks: frequency counting, order-preserving deduplication, and an O(1) least-recently-used cache.

sections.heading: Frequency counts
sections.body:
Counting is the most common hashing pattern: one pass, O(n) expected time.

- `Counter(iterable)` counts hashable items. `most_common(k)` returns the k largest counts; equal counts are ordered by first appearance. `Counter('abracadabra').most_common(3)` is `[('a', 5), ('b', 2), ('r', 2)]`.
- Counter arithmetic: `c - d` keeps only positive counts, `c & d` takes minimums and `c | d` takes maximums. Two strings are anagrams when their Counters are equal.
- `defaultdict(int)` or `defaultdict(list)` supplies a default on first access. The `default_factory` runs only through `d[key]` (`__getitem__`). `d.get(key)` returns None and inserts nothing, and `key in d` does not insert either. Reading `d[key]` just to test it **creates** the key.

Grouping (anagram groups, events per user) is the same pattern with a list as the value and a canonical key such as `tuple(sorted(word))`.

sections.heading: Deduplication and membership
sections.body:
A `set` answers "have I seen this?" in O(1) average, versus O(n) for `x in some_list`. Turning an O(n) list scan inside a loop into a set lookup changes an O(n·m) algorithm into O(n + m).

Set iteration order is **not** guaranteed, so `list(set(items))` loses the original order (and for strings varies between runs because of hash randomization). Dicts preserve insertion order as a language guarantee, so `list(dict.fromkeys(items))` deduplicates while keeping first occurrences. A loop with a `seen` set that appends unseen items does the same and lets you dedupe by a derived key, such as a lowercased email address.

sections.heading: LRU cache with a hash map and a doubly linked list
sections.body:
A **least-recently-used cache** with capacity c needs `get` and `put` in O(1), and evicts the least recently used entry when full. No single structure does all of that:

- A **hash map** from key to node finds an entry in O(1).
- A **doubly linked list** ordered by recency moves a node to the front, or removes the tail, in O(1) once you hold the node.

On `get`: look up the node, unlink it, relink it at the most-recent end. On `put`: update or insert at the most-recent end; if the size exceeds c, remove the node at the least-recent end and delete its key from the map (so each node also stores its key). The list must be doubly linked because unlinking a node needs its predecessor.

A singly linked list, a plain list (O(n) removal from the middle) or a heap keyed by timestamp (O(log n), and stale entries) all miss the O(1) target.

sections.heading: LRU in Python: OrderedDict and functools

keyPoints: Counter.most_common orders ties by first appearance.
defaultdict inserts only on d[key]; get and in do not insert.
list(dict.fromkeys(x)) dedupes while preserving order; list(set(x)) does not.
LRU = hash map (find node) + doubly linked list (reorder and evict) for O(1) get and put.
OrderedDict: move_to_end on access, popitem(last=False) to evict.

gotchas.trap: Testing if d[key]: on a defaultdict is harmless.
gotchas.correct: It inserts key with the default value. Use key in d or d.get(key).

gotchas.trap: OrderedDict.popitem() evicts the least recently used item.
gotchas.correct: popitem() defaults to last=True and pops the most recent end. Use popitem(last=False).

gotchas.trap: lru_cache works on any function.
gotchas.correct: All arguments must be hashable; a list argument raises TypeError.

Drive both with the same 10,000 random get/put operations and a capacity of 50, and assert that they return identical results. Finally wrap a recursive Fibonacci in `functools.cache`, compute `[fib(n) for n in range(16)]` and read `fib.cache_info()`.

lessons.title: Binary trees: traversals, height and recursion
lessons.summary: How to walk a binary tree in pre-, in-, post- and level order, how to compute height and other properties recursively, and when to switch to an explicit stack because Python recursion is shallow.

sections.heading: Nodes, depth and height
The four traversals
sections.body:
Depth-first traversals differ only in *when* the node itself is visited relative to its subtrees:

| Traversal | Order | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| Preorder | node, left, right | copy or serialise a tree |
| Inorder | left, node, right | keys in sorted order for a BST |
| Postorder | left, right, node | free or aggregate children first (sizes, heights, deleting) |
| Level order | by depth, left to right | shortest number of edges, printing by level |

For the tree with root 8, left subtree 3 -> (1, 6 -> (4, 7)) and right subtree 10 -> (none, 14 -> (13, none)):

- preorder: `[8, 3, 1, 6, 4, 7, 10, 14, 13]`
- inorder: `[1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 13, 14]` (sorted, because it is a BST)
- postorder: `[1, 4, 7, 6, 3, 13, 14, 10, 8]`
- level order: `[8, 3, 10, 1, 6, 14, 4, 7, 13]`

Each traversal visits every node once, so it runs in O(n) time. Recursive DFS uses O(h) stack space; level order uses a queue that can hold a whole level, up to about n/2 nodes.

sections.heading: Level order needs a real queue
sections.body:
Breadth-first traversal is a queue algorithm. Use `collections.deque`, whose `popleft()` is O(1). A list with `pop(0)` shifts every remaining element, which turns an O(n) traversal into O(n^2).

```python
from collections import deque

def level_order(root):
    out, q = [], deque([root] if root else [])
    while q:
        node = q.popleft()
        out.append(node.val)
        for child in (node.left, node.right):
            if child:
                q.append(child)
    return out
```

To group by level, process `len(q)` nodes per outer iteration.

sections.heading: Recursion depth and iterative traversal
sections.body:
CPython's default recursion limit (`sys.getrecursionlimit()`) is 1000. A recursive traversal of a degenerate tree with 10,000 nodes raises `RecursionError`. Real inputs that arrive sorted produce exactly that chain shape in an unbalanced BST.

An explicit stack removes the limit:

```python
def inorder_iter(root):
    out, stack, node = [], [], root
    while stack or node:
        while node:
            stack.append(node)
            node = node.left
        node = stack.pop()
        out.append(node.val)
        node = node.right
    return out
```

Raising the limit with `sys.setrecursionlimit` is only a stopgap: very deep recursion still costs a lot of memory, can crash the interpreter on some platforms, and leaves the O(n) height problem in place.

sections.heading: Rebuilding and recognising trees
sections.body:
With distinct keys, **preorder plus inorder** (or postorder plus inorder) determines a binary tree uniquely: the first preorder element is the root, and its position in the inorder list splits the left and right subtrees. Preorder plus postorder is not enough in general, because a node with a single child looks the same whether that child is on the left or the right.

Many tree problems follow one recursive template: solve both subtrees, then combine at the node (postorder). Height, size, diameter, "is balanced" and subtree sums all fit it.

keyPoints: Tree operations cost O(h); h ranges from about lg n (balanced) to n - 1 (a chain).
Inorder traversal of a BST yields keys in sorted order.
Level order uses a FIFO queue: collections.deque with popleft(), not list.pop(0).
Python's default recursion limit is 1000, so deep or degenerate trees need an explicit stack.
Preorder + inorder with distinct keys reconstructs a unique tree; preorder + postorder does not in general.

gotchas.trap: Using list.pop(0) as the queue for level-order traversal.
gotchas.correct: Use collections.deque and popleft(), which is O(1) at either end.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a recursive traversal is safe for any input size.
gotchas.correct: A chain-shaped tree deeper than about 1000 nodes raises RecursionError; use an explicit stack or queue.

gotchas.trap: Mixing height conventions (nodes versus edges) inside one solution.
gotchas.correct: Pick one convention, for example empty = -1 and leaf = 0 in edges, and use it consistently.

lessons.lab: Build the 9-node example tree from the traversals section. Write recursive preorder, inorder and postorder functions and an iterative level order with deque, and check that they print the four lists shown. Then insert 1..5000 in increasing order into a plain BST, call your recursive height function and observe RecursionError; rewrite height iteratively with a level-order loop and confirm it returns 4999.

lessons.title: Binary search trees and balanced trees
lessons.summary: The BST ordering invariant, why insertion order decides performance, and how AVL and red-black trees keep height logarithmic. Ends with what Python offers instead of a built-in balanced tree.

sections.heading: The BST invariant
Insertion order decides the shape
sections.body:
Algorithms, 4th ed. shows that a BST built from N keys inserted in **random** order needs about 2 ln N (about 1.39 lg N) compares on average for a search hit or miss. In the worst case (keys inserted in sorted order) the tree becomes a chain and every operation costs O(N).

Sorted or nearly sorted input is common in practice: timestamps, auto-increment ids, a file that was already sorted. A plain BST is therefore risky whenever you do not control insertion order.

sections.heading: Ordered operations a hash table lacks
sections.body:
A BST keeps keys in order, which makes these operations cheap (O(h)):

- **floor / ceiling**: largest key <= x, smallest key >= x
- **rank / select**: how many keys are below x; the k-th smallest key (with subtree sizes stored in nodes)
- **range queries**: all keys in [lo, hi], in sorted order
- **min / max** and sorted iteration (inorder)

A hash table gives average O(1) exact lookup but none of these without scanning everything. Choose a BST (or a sorted structure) when the workload needs order.

sections.heading: AVL trees
sections.body:
An AVL tree (MIT 6.006, lecture 7) stores a height in every node and keeps the **balance factor**, height(right) - height(left), in {-1, 0, +1} at every node. After an insert or delete, the heights along the changed path are updated and any node that goes out of range is fixed with one or two **rotations**. A rotation is a constant-time local rearrangement that preserves the inorder sequence (and so the BST invariant).

The balance condition forces height O(log n), so search, insert and delete are O(log n) in the worst case.

sections.heading: Red-black trees (left-leaning)
sections.body:
Algorithms, 4th ed. derives red-black BSTs from **2-3 trees**, where a node may hold one or two keys and all leaves sit at the same depth. A left-leaning red-black BST encodes each 3-node as two binary nodes joined by a red link that leans left. Insertion uses rotations and colour flips to keep perfect **black balance**.

Guarantees from that chapter: height is at most 2 lg N, the average path to a node is about 1.00 lg N, and search, insert, delete, min, max, floor, ceiling, rank, select and range count are all logarithmic in the worst case. Ordered maps in several other languages' standard libraries (for example Java's TreeMap) are built on red-black trees.

sections.heading: What to use in Python
sections.body:
Python has no built-in balanced BST. Common substitutes:

| Need | Structure | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Exact membership only | `set` / `dict` | O(1) average |
| Repeated min (or max via negation) | `heapq` | O(log n) push/pop |
| Floor, ceiling, ranges; mostly reads | sorted `list` + `bisect` | O(log n) search, O(n) insert |

Floor with bisect: `i = bisect_right(a, x)`; if `i > 0`, the floor is `a[i - 1]`. `insort` finds the position in O(log n) but the list shift is O(n), so heavy insert workloads at large n need a real balanced tree (implemented yourself or from a third-party package).

keyPoints: The BST invariant covers whole subtrees, not just a node's direct children.
Random insertion order gives about 1.39 lg N compares on average; sorted insertion gives a chain with O(N) operations.
BSTs support ordered queries (floor, ceiling, rank, select, range) that hash tables cannot answer efficiently.
AVL trees keep each balance factor in {-1, 0, +1} using rotations; red-black trees keep perfect black balance with height at most 2 lg N.
Rotations take O(1) time and preserve the inorder order of keys.
Python has no built-in balanced BST; sorted list + bisect gives O(log n) search but O(n) insert.

gotchas.trap: Validating a BST by checking only node.left.val < node.val < node.right.val.
gotchas.correct: Pass lower and upper bounds down the recursion, or check that the inorder sequence is strictly increasing.

gotchas.trap: Assuming BST operations are O(log n) by default.
gotchas.correct: They are O(h). Without balancing, sorted input makes h = n - 1.

gotchas.trap: Believing bisect.insort makes inserts O(log n).
gotchas.correct: The search is O(log n), but shifting list elements makes each insert O(n).

lessons.lab: Insert 2000 keys into an unbalanced BST twice: once in sorted order and once after random.shuffle. Measure the height of each (iteratively). Then implement floor(x) with a sorted list and bisect_right, and check it against a brute-force max(k for k in keys if k <= x) on 1000 random queries.

lessons.title: Heaps and priority queues with heapq
lessons.summary: The binary-heap invariant, why heapify is linear while n pushes are O(n log n), and the heapq patterns that come up constantly: top-k, k-way merge, max-heaps by negation and safe tie-breaking.

sections.heading: The heap invariant in an array
sections.body:
A binary min-heap is a complete binary tree stored in a list. In `heapq`'s 0-based layout, the children of index k are 2k+1 and 2k+2, and the invariant is `heap[k] <= heap[2k+1]` and `heap[k] <= heap[2k+2]`. So `heap[0]` is always the smallest item.

The list is **not** sorted. `heapq.heapify([5, 3, 8, 1, 9, 2])` gives `[1, 3, 2, 5, 9, 8]`: the minimum is first, but iterating the list does not give sorted order. Only repeated `heappop` does.

`heapq` compares items with `<` only, and its heap is a min-heap.

sections.heading: Costs
sections.body:
| Operation | heapq call | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Peek min | `heap[0]` | O(1) |
| Push | `heappush(h, x)` | O(log n) |
| Pop min | `heappop(h)` | O(log n); IndexError if empty |
| Push then pop | `heappushpop(h, x)` | O(log n), faster than the two calls |
| Pop then push | `heapreplace(h, x)` | O(log n) |
| Build from list | `heapify(h)` | O(n), in place |

Why is heapify linear? Bottom-up heap construction sifts each internal node down; most nodes are near the bottom and move only a short distance, and the sum of those distances is O(n). Pushing n items one by one is O(n log n) in the worst case. MIT 6.006 lecture 8 and Algorithms 4th ed. section 2.4 develop both.

`heappushpop(h, x)` returns x itself if x is no larger than the current minimum. `heapreplace(h, x)` always pops the old minimum first, so it can return a value larger than x. With `h = [1, 5, 3]`, `heapreplace(h, 0)` returns 1, while `heappushpop(h, 0)` returns 0 and leaves h unchanged.

sections.heading: Max-heaps on Python 3.13
sections.body:
The current Python docs list `heappush_max`, `heappop_max` and related functions, but those were **added in 3.14**. On 3.13 they do not exist. Build a max-heap by negating keys:

```python
import heapq
h = []
for x in [5, 3, 8, 1]:
    heapq.heappush(h, -x)
print(-heapq.heappop(h))   # 8
```

For records, push `(-priority, ...)` tuples.

sections.heading: Tie-breaking and lazy deletion
sections.body:
Tuples compare element by element. If two entries have equal priority, Python compares the next field. Pushing `(1, {"a": 1})` and `(1, {"b": 2})` raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'dict' and 'dict'`.

The heapq docs' fix is a monotonically increasing counter as the second field, so tasks are never compared and equal priorities pop in insertion order:

```python
import heapq, itertools
counter = itertools.count()
heapq.heappush(pq, (priority, next(counter), task))
```

heapq has no decrease-key or arbitrary delete. The docs recommend **lazy deletion**: keep a dict from task to its entry, mark a removed entry as REMOVED, and skip such entries when they reach the top. Dijkstra in Python uses the same idea by pushing duplicates and skipping stale ones. An alternative to tuples is `@dataclass(order=True)` with the payload declared `field(compare=False)`.

sections.heading: Top-k and k-way merge

keyPoints: heapq is a min-heap: heap[0] is the smallest, children of k are 2k+1 and 2k+2.
A heap list is not sorted; only repeated heappop yields sorted order.
heapify is O(n); n separate pushes are O(n log n); push and pop are O(log n).
On Python 3.13 build max-heaps by negating keys; the *_max functions arrived in 3.14.
Use (priority, count, task) entries so equal priorities never compare the task.
Top-k with a size-k heap is O(n log k); heapq.merge of k sorted inputs is O(N log k) and lazy.

gotchas.correct: Only heap[0] is guaranteed; pop repeatedly or call sorted() for full order.

gotchas.trap: Calling heapq.heappush_max on Python 3.13.
gotchas.correct: It does not exist before 3.14; push negated keys instead.

gotchas.trap: Pushing (priority, task) where tasks are dicts or custom objects.
gotchas.correct: Insert a tie-breaking counter: (priority, next(counter), task).

gotchas.trap: Sorting all n items to get the top 10.
gotchas.correct: Use a size-k heap or heapq.nlargest for O(n log k).

Then write a scheduler that pushes dict tasks with equal priorities and reproduce the TypeError; fix it with itertools.count().

lessons.title: Tries, union-find, segment trees and Fenwick trees
lessons.summary: Four specialised structures that turn slow scans into fast queries: tries for prefix search, union-find for dynamic connectivity, and segment and Fenwick trees for range queries with updates.

sections.heading: Tries for prefix search
sections.body:
A trie stores strings character by character along root-to-node paths. Each node maps a character to a child and carries an **end-of-word marker**. Searching or inserting a key of length L takes O(L) steps no matter how many keys are stored, and listing every key with a given prefix costs O(L) to reach the prefix node plus the size of the subtree below it. Algorithms, 4th ed. (section 5.2) covers R-way tries and ternary search tries, including prefix and wildcard matching.

```python
def insert(root, word):
    node = root
    for ch in word:
        node = node.setdefault(ch, {})
    node["$"] = True          # end-of-word marker

def contains(root, word):
    node = root
    for ch in word:
        if ch not in node:
            return False
        node = node[ch]
    return "$" in node        # a path alone is not a word
```

After inserting only `cart` and `care`, the path `c-a-r` exists but `contains(root, "car")` is False. Forgetting the marker is the classic trie bug.

**Memory:** an R-way trie with an array of R child links per node wastes space for large alphabets. Dict children (as above) or a ternary search trie (TST) store only the links that exist. For a static word list, a sorted list plus `bisect_left(words, prefix)` and a forward scan while `startswith(prefix)` is a simple alternative.

sections.heading: Union-find (disjoint sets)
sections.body:
Union-find keeps a partition of n items into disjoint sets with two operations: `find(x)` returns the set's representative (root) and `union(a, b)` merges two sets. It answers "are a and b connected?" for a graph that only gains edges, and it is the cycle check inside Kruskal's MST algorithm.

Algorithms, 4th ed. (section 1.5) compares implementations:

- **Quick-find:** find is O(1) but each union scans the whole array (between n + 3 and 2n + 1 array accesses).
- **Quick-union:** link one root under another. Without care the trees become chains, so find can be O(n).
- **Weighted quick-union** (union by size; union by rank is the CLRS variant with the same bounds): link the smaller tree under the larger. Depth is at most lg n, so operations are O(log n) worst case.
- **Plus path compression:** point nodes on the find path at the root. The amortized cost per operation is bounded by the inverse Ackermann function, less than 5 for any practical n.

```python
parent = list(range(n)); size = [1] * n
def find(x):
    root = x
    while parent[root] != root:
        root = parent[root]
    while parent[x] != root:            # path compression
        parent[x], x = root, parent[x]
    return root
def union(a, b):
    ra, rb = find(a), find(b)
    if ra == rb:
        return False                     # already connected (a cycle in Kruskal)
    if size[ra] < size[rb]:
        ra, rb = rb, ra
    parent[rb] = ra; size[ra] += size[rb]
    return True
```

Union-find does not support splitting sets or deleting edges efficiently.

sections.heading: Range queries: why prefix sums are not enough
sections.body: For a static array, a prefix-sum array (`itertools.accumulate`) answers any range sum in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing: sum(l..r) = P[r+1] - P[l]. But a single point update forces O(n) work to rebuild the prefixes. When updates and queries are interleaved, you want both in O(log n). The two standard tools are segment trees and Fenwick trees. (The facts below are standard results stated from first principles; MIT 6.046 covers the related idea of range trees.)

sections.heading: Fenwick (binary indexed) tree
sections.body:
A Fenwick tree is a single array t[1..n]. Entry t[i] holds the sum of the block of length `i & -i` (the lowest set bit of i) that ends at i. For example, `12 & -12` is 4, so t[12] covers indices 9..12.

```python
class Fenwick:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.t = [0] * (n + 1)        # 1-based
    def add(self, i, delta):          # a[i] += delta
        while i < len(self.t):
            self.t[i] += delta
            i += i & -i
    def prefix(self, i):              # a[1] + ... + a[i]
        s = 0
        while i > 0:
            s += self.t[i]
            i -= i & -i
        return s
```

Both loops run O(log n) times. A range sum is `prefix(r) - prefix(l - 1)`, which relies on subtraction, so the Fenwick tree fits invertible operations such as sums and counts. For the array 3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6 (1-based), `prefix(5)` is 14 and the sum of positions 3..7 is 21.

sections.heading: Segment tree
sections.body:
A segment tree is a binary tree over the index range. The root covers [0, n), each node covers a range split in half between its children, and each node stores the aggregate (sum, min, max, gcd, ...) of its range. It has O(n) nodes and builds in O(n).

- **Point update:** change a leaf and recompute the O(log n) ancestors.
- **Range query:** any range decomposes into O(log n) fully covered nodes.

Because it combines node values directly instead of subtracting prefixes, a segment tree works for any associative operation, including min and max, which a plain Fenwick tree cannot answer for arbitrary ranges. With **lazy propagation** it also supports range updates.

| Structure | Build | Point update | Range query | Operations |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Prefix sums | O(n) | O(n) | O(1) | invertible (sum) |
| Fenwick tree | O(n log n) simple, O(n) possible | O(log n) | O(log n) | invertible (sum, count) |
| Segment tree | O(n) | O(log n) | O(log n) | any associative (sum, min, max) |

keyPoints: Trie search and insert cost O(L) for a key of length L, independent of the number of keys.
A trie needs an end-of-word marker; an existing path is not proof that a word was inserted.
Weighted quick-union keeps depth at most lg n; adding path compression makes the amortized cost nearly constant (inverse Ackermann).
Union-find merges sets and tests connectivity; it cannot efficiently split sets or remove edges.
Prefix sums give O(1) range sums but O(n) updates; Fenwick and segment trees give O(log n) for both.
Fenwick trees need an invertible operation (sum); segment trees handle any associative operation, such as range min.

gotchas.trap: Treating any existing trie path as a stored word.
gotchas.correct: Check the end-of-word marker at the final node.

gotchas.trap: Plain quick-union without union by size/rank.
gotchas.correct: Link the smaller tree under the larger, and compress paths during find.

gotchas.trap: Rebuilding a prefix-sum array after every update in an update-heavy workload.
gotchas.correct: Use a Fenwick tree or segment tree for O(log n) updates and queries.

gotchas.trap: Using a Fenwick tree for arbitrary range minimum.
gotchas.correct: Range min is not invertible; use a segment tree (or a sparse table if the array is static).

lessons.lab: Implement the Fenwick class above and a brute-force list; apply 10,000 random point updates and range-sum queries to both and assert they agree. Then implement union-find with size and path compression, union random pairs among 100,000 items, and compare the count of components to a BFS over the same edges.

lessons.title: Comparison sorts and the n log n lower bound
lessons.summary: How mergesort, quicksort and heapsort trade off worst-case time, extra space and stability, and why no comparison sort can beat about n lg n compares.

sections.heading: Mergesort: guaranteed n log n, linear extra space
sections.body:
Mergesort splits the array in half, sorts each half recursively, and merges the two sorted halves. Its recurrence is $$T(n) = 2T(n/2) + \Theta(n)$$, which solves to $$\Theta(n \log n)$$.

Princeton's algs4 states that top-down mergesort uses between ½ N lg N and N lg N compares, and that it needs **extra space proportional to N** for the auxiliary array. The merge step takes from the left half when keys are equal, so mergesort is **stable**.

```python
def merge_sort(a):
    if len(a) <= 1:
        return a
    mid = len(a) // 2
    left, right = merge_sort(a[:mid]), merge_sort(a[mid:])
    out, i, j = [], 0, 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if right[j] < left[i]:   # strict: ties take from left, keeping stability
            out.append(right[j]); j += 1
        else:
            out.append(left[i]); i += 1
    out.extend(left[i:]); out.extend(right[j:])
    return out
```

sections.heading: Quicksort: fast in practice, quadratic in the worst case
sections.body:
Quicksort partitions around a pivot, then recurses on the two sides. It sorts in place with only a small recursion stack. algs4 gives about **2 N ln N (≈ 1.39 N lg N) compares on average** and about **N²/2 in the worst case**. The worst case appears when the pivot is always the smallest or largest key, for example a first-element pivot on already sorted input.

The practical defences are:

- **Shuffle the input (or pick a random pivot)** so the bad case is vanishingly unlikely for any input. MIT 6.046 analyses this randomized quicksort.
- **Cut off to insertion sort** for small subarrays (algs4 suggests sizes between 5 and 15).
- **3-way partitioning** (Dijkstra's Dutch national flag) splits into `< pivot`, `== pivot` and `> pivot`. With many duplicate keys, standard 2-way partitioning wastes work, while 3-way partitioning is entropy-optimal.

Standard in-place quicksort is **not stable**, because long-distance swaps can reorder equal keys.

sections.heading: Heapsort: in place and worst-case n log n, but not stable
sections.body:
Heapsort builds a heap in linear time, then repeatedly removes the maximum (or minimum) at O(log n) each. That gives **O(n log n) in the worst case with O(1) extra space**. It is not stable, and the Python heapq docs say the same about heapsort built from heapq. Its memory access pattern jumps around the array, so it is usually slower in practice than a good quicksort or mergesort.

In Python you can write heapsort with `heapq.heapify` plus repeated `heappop`, but `sorted()` is faster and stable. Treat heapsort as the answer when the question demands both a worst-case guarantee and constant extra space.

sections.heading: Stability and why it matters
sections.body:
A sort is **stable** if records with equal keys keep their original relative order. Stability lets you sort by several keys in passes: sort by the secondary key first, then stably by the primary key. Within each primary group, the secondary order survives.

| Algorithm | Worst case | Extra space | Stable |
|---|---|---|---|
| Insertion sort | O(n²) | O(1) | yes |
| Mergesort | O(n log n) | O(n) | yes |
| Quicksort (random pivot) | O(n²), expected O(n log n) | O(log n) stack | no |
| Heapsort | O(n log n) | O(1) | no |
| Python `sorted` / `list.sort` | O(n log n) | up to O(n) | yes (guaranteed) |

sections.heading: The comparison lower bound
sections.body:
A comparison sort learns about the input only through yes/no comparisons. Model it as a binary decision tree. Each of the n! input orderings must reach a different leaf, so the tree needs at least n! leaves and height at least $$\log_2(n!)$$. By Stirling's approximation, $$\log_2(n!) = \Theta(n \log n)$$.

So **every comparison-based sort needs Ω(n log n) compares in the worst case**, and algs4 calls mergesort "asymptotically optimal" for this reason. The bound does not apply to algorithms that inspect key digits or use keys as array indices, such as counting sort and radix sort. Those can run in linear time when the key range or digit count is bounded.

keyPoints: Mergesort: Θ(n log n) always, O(n) extra space, stable.
Quicksort: expected ~1.39 n lg n compares, worst case ~n²/2; shuffle or randomize the pivot to avoid it.
3-way partitioning makes quicksort efficient on inputs with many duplicate keys.
Heapsort: O(n log n) worst case in O(1) extra space, but not stable and slower in practice.
Any comparison sort needs at least lg(n!) = Θ(n log n) compares in the worst case.

gotchas.trap: Quicksort is O(n log n), so it is always safe on adversarial or pre-sorted input.
gotchas.correct: Deterministic quicksort with a fixed pivot rule is O(n²) on bad inputs such as sorted data with a first-element pivot. Randomize (shuffle or random pivot) to get expected O(n log n).

gotchas.trap: A clever comparison sort can reach O(n) worst case on arbitrary keys.
gotchas.correct: The decision-tree argument rules this out: lg(n!) = Θ(n log n). Linear time needs a non-comparison method and assumptions about the keys.

gotchas.trap: Heapsort is a good choice when you need a stable sort.
gotchas.correct: Heapsort is not stable. Use mergesort or Python's built-in sort when equal keys must keep their order.

lessons.lab: Using only the standard library, implement `merge_sort` and a quicksort that always takes `a[0]` as its pivot. Count comparisons on `list(range(2000))` and on a shuffled copy. Then add `random.shuffle` before quicksort and compare again. Finally sort `[(k % 3, i) for i, k in enumerate(range(12))]` by the first field with your mergesort and check that the second field stays increasing inside each group.

lessons.title: Linear-time sorts and sorting in Python
lessons.summary: Counting sort and LSD radix sort beat the comparison bound by using key structure. Python's built-in sort is a stable, adaptive merge sort driven by key functions.

sections.heading: Counting sort
sections.body:
When keys are small integers in a range `0..k-1`, count how many times each key occurs, turn the counts into starting positions with a prefix sum, and place each record into its slot. This takes **O(n + k)** time and O(n + k) space. Placing records in input order (left to right, using the starting positions) makes counting sort **stable**.

Counting sort is a good fit when k is O(n), such as ages 0 to 120 or exam scores 0 to 100. It is a poor fit when k is huge, such as arbitrary 64-bit integers, because the count array becomes enormous.

```python
def counting_sort(records, key, k):
    count = [0] * (k + 1)
    for r in records:
        count[key(r) + 1] += 1
    for i in range(k):            # prefix sums -> start index of each key
        count[i + 1] += count[i]
    out = [None] * len(records)
    for r in records:             # left to right keeps it stable
        out[count[key(r)]] = r
        count[key(r)] += 1
    return out
```

sections.heading: Radix sort
sections.body:
LSD (least-significant-digit-first) radix sort sorts fixed-width keys one digit at a time, from the rightmost digit to the leftmost, using a **stable** sort such as counting sort for each pass. Stability is essential: after sorting by digit d, ties must keep the order produced by the earlier, less significant digits.

With w digits in base R, the cost is **O(w · (n + R))**. MIT 6.006 presents this as sorting integers in a range up to n^c in linear time by choosing base n. algs4 Section 5.1 covers LSD and MSD string sorts.

sections.heading: Python's built-in sort
sections.body:
`list.sort()` sorts in place and returns `None`. `sorted()` takes any iterable and returns a new list. The Sorting HOWTO says: "Sorts are guaranteed to be stable", and the sort uses only `<` comparisons between items.

The algorithm is **Timsort**: an adaptive, stable natural merge sort that finds runs already present in the data and merges them. Recent CPython uses the powersort merge policy, but the docs still call it Timsort. It is O(n log n) in the worst case, and the Python time-complexity page notes it is adaptive: already sorted or reverse-sorted input needs only O(n) comparisons.

sections.heading: Key functions, reverse and multi-pass sorts
sections.body:
Pass `key=` to sort by a derived value. The HOWTO says the key function "is called exactly once for each input record", so an expensive key is computed n times, not once per comparison.

```python
sorted(["b", "A", "a"], key=str.lower)      # ['A', 'a', 'b']  (stable: 'A' stays before 'a')

rows = [("bob", 30), ("amy", 25), ("cat", 30), ("dan", 25)]
rows.sort(key=lambda r: r[0])                 # secondary key first
rows.sort(key=lambda r: r[1], reverse=True)   # then primary
# [('bob', 30), ('cat', 30), ('amy', 25), ('dan', 25)]
```

`reverse=True` still keeps equal records in their original order. A tuple key such as `key=lambda r: (-r[1], r[0])` does the same job in one pass when every field can be negated or compared directly. For an old-style two-argument comparator, wrap it with `functools.cmp_to_key`.

keyPoints: Counting sort is O(n + k) and stable; use it when the key range k is small relative to n.
LSD radix sort runs a stable sort per digit from least to most significant: O(w(n + R)).
Python's sort is stable, adaptive Timsort; nearly sorted data sorts in close to linear time.
The key function runs once per element; multi-key sorts work by sorting secondary first, then primary.
functools.cmp_to_key adapts a comparator function into a key.

gotchas.trap: Radix sort works with any per-digit sort, so use the fastest unstable one.
gotchas.correct: LSD radix sort is only correct if each digit pass is stable; an unstable pass destroys the order from earlier digits.

gotchas.trap: `reverse=True` reverses the order of equal elements too.
gotchas.correct: The HOWTO states that reverse sorts keep stability: equal records retain their original relative order.

gotchas.trap: `x = x.sort()` gives you the sorted list.
gotchas.correct: `list.sort()` sorts in place and returns None. Use `sorted(x)` for a new list.

lessons.lab: Write `counting_sort` for records `(name, score)` with scores 0..100 and check it matches `sorted(records, key=lambda r: r[1])` exactly, including tie order. Then build an LSD radix sort for 6-digit non-negative integers using your counting sort per decimal digit, and compare against `sorted()` on 10,000 random values. Finally replace one digit pass with an unstable placement (iterate the input backwards) and observe the wrong output.
