questions.stem: A proof charges each append 3 units: 1 pays for writing the new element and 2 are stored as credit on the array, and those stored credits pay for copying elements when the array doubles. Which technique is this, and what must the proof show?
options: Accounting method; it must show the stored credit never goes negative.
Aggregate method; it must show the average input is random.
Potential method; it must show the potential decreases on every operation.
Probabilistic analysis; it must show resizes occur with low probability.
questions.explanation: Charging a fixed fee per operation and saving the surplus as credit is the accounting (banker's) method. The bound holds as long as the credit balance is never negative, because then the total charged is an upper bound on the actual cost.
rationales: Correct. A non-negative credit balance means the charges cover all actual costs.
The aggregate method bounds the total directly and makes no assumption about random input.
In the potential method potential rises on cheap operations; it does not decrease on every step.
Amortized analysis involves no probability.

questions.scenario: A product manager reads that `list.append` is "O(1) amortized" and concludes that a latency-critical loop doing one append per request will never have a slow request caused by append.
questions.stem: What is the most accurate response?
options: Correct; amortized O(1) means every single append is O(1).
Incorrect; amortized means average over random inputs, so some inputs are slow.
Incorrect; an individual append can take O(n) when the list resizes. Amortized O(1) bounds the total over the sequence, not each operation.
Correct; the resize cost is paid by the operating system rather than by the request.
questions.explanation: The official cost table notes that an individual amortized operation may occasionally be O(n) when the underlying storage is resized, with the cost spread over many operations. Amortized bounds are about totals over a sequence, so a single request can still see a resize spike.
rationales: Amortized is weaker than a per-operation worst-case bound.
Amortized analysis involves no probability or random input; it is a worst-case bound on sequences.
Correct. Occasional O(n) resizes are what the amortized bound averages away.
The interpreter copies the elements itself, inside the append call.

questions.stem: Merge sort splits a list into two halves, sorts each recursively, and merges the results in linear time. Which recurrence and solution describe its running time?
options: $$T(n)=2T(n/2)+n$$, so $$\Theta(n\log n)$$
questions.explanation: There are two subcalls on half-size inputs plus linear merging, so $$a=2$$, $$b=2$$, $$f(n)=n=n^{\log_2 2}$$. That is master theorem case 2, giving $$\Theta(n\log n)$$, and the recursion tree confirms it with $$\log n$$ levels of $$n$$ work each.
rationales: This leaves out the linear merge cost.
Merge sort halves the input; it does not recurse on n - 1 twice.
That recurrence has one subcall, which describes something like quickselect's good case, not merge sort.
Correct. Every level of the recursion tree does n work across log n levels.

sources.title: Sorting and merge sort — MIT 6.006 Spring 2020

questions.stem: A divide-and-conquer matrix algorithm makes 8 recursive calls on half-size problems and does $$\Theta(n^2)$$ extra work per call: $$T(n)=8T(n/2)+n^2$$. What is $$T(n)$$?
options: $$\Theta(n^2\log n)$$
$$\Theta(n^3)$$
$$\Theta(n^8)$$
$$\Theta(n^2)$$
questions.explanation: Here $$n^{\log_b a}=n^{\log_2 8}=n^3$$, and $$f(n)=n^2$$ is polynomially smaller. That is master theorem case 1: the leaves dominate and $$T(n)=\Theta(n^3)$$.
rationales: The log factor appears only when f(n) matches n^(log_b a).
Correct. Case 1, where leaf work n^(log_2 8) dominates.
The exponent is log_2 8 = 3, not a = 8.
That would require the root's work to dominate, but f(n) is smaller than n^3.

questions.scenario: A recursive function removes the first element of its input, does a linear scan of the remainder, and recurses on the remainder: $$T(n)=T(n-1)+n$$. A teammate wants to apply the master theorem.
questions.stem: What is the right way to solve this recurrence, and what is the result?
options: The master theorem does not apply; summing the recursion tree gives n + (n-1) + ... + 1 = Theta(n^2).
Master theorem case 2 with a = 1, b = 1, giving Theta(n log n).
Master theorem case 3, giving Theta(n).
It cannot be solved; subtract-and-conquer recurrences have no closed form.
questions.explanation: The master theorem requires subproblems of size $$n/b$$ with $$b>1$$, which $$n-1$$ is not. The recursion tree is a single chain whose levels cost $$n, n-1, \dots, 1$$, summing to $$n(n+1)/2=\Theta(n^2)$$.
rationales: Correct. Use a recursion tree or substitution for subtract-and-conquer.
b must be greater than 1; with b = 1 log_b a is undefined.
The theorem does not apply, and the work is clearly more than linear.
It has a simple closed form found by summing the levels.

questions.scenario: A recursive DFS works on small test graphs, but on a production graph that is essentially a 50,000-node chain it crashes with `RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded` under CPython 3.13.
questions.stem: What is the most robust fix?
options: Call `sys.setrecursionlimit(10**9)` at startup.
Wrap the call in `try/except RecursionError` and return a partial result.
Rewrite the DFS iteratively with an explicit stack.
Mark the function as tail-recursive so CPython reuses the frame.
questions.explanation: CPython's default recursion limit is 1000, and DFS on a chain recurses once per node. An explicit stack keeps the traversal on the heap, so its depth is limited only by memory, whereas the `sys` docs warn that a too-high recursion limit can lead to a crash.
rationales: The sys docs warn that a too-high limit can lead to a crash, and the safe maximum is platform-dependent; it moves the ceiling instead of removing it.
That silently returns wrong results for exactly the inputs that matter.
Correct. An explicit stack removes the dependence on the call-stack depth.
CPython performs no tail-call elimination, and DFS is not tail recursive anyway.

questions.stem: Which reasoning identifies the defect and the fix?
options: Python integers overflow on large sums; use `math.fsum`.
For a one-element list, mid is 0 and `a[mid:]` is the whole list again, so the subproblem is not smaller; add a base case for `len(a) == 1`.
The base case should be `if len(a) == 0: return None`.
The slices copy data, so the function is too slow; pass indices instead.
questions.explanation: An inductive correctness argument requires every recursive call to be on a strictly smaller input. With one element, `a[0:]` is the same length, so recursion never reaches the base case. Returning `a[0]` when the length is 1 restores progress.
rationales: Python ints are arbitrary precision and do not overflow.
Correct. The inductive step fails because the subproblem does not shrink.
Returning None would break the addition and still leaves the length-1 case recursing forever.
Slicing costs time, but that is not why the function never terminates.

questions.stem:
Consider this loop:

```python
best = a[0]
for i in range(1, len(a)):
    if a[i] > best:
        best = a[i]
```

Which loop invariant proves that `best` is the maximum of the list when the loop ends?
options: `best >= a[i]` at the start of every iteration.
`i` increases by 1 on every iteration.
`best` is an element of `a`.
At the start of the iteration with index `i`, `best == max(a[:i])`.
questions.explanation: This invariant holds initially (i = 1, best = a[0]), each iteration preserves it, and at exit i = len(a), so it says best = max(a). A valid invariant must give the desired result at termination, not merely stay true.
rationales: This is false before any iteration where a[i] exceeds the current best.
That describes progress, not what the loop computes.
True throughout, but it does not imply best is the maximum.
Correct. It covers initialization, maintenance and a useful termination step.

questions.scenario: You are writing tests for a new `lower_bound(a, x)` function that returns the first index in a sorted list `a` whose value is at least `x`.
questions.stem: Which test inputs target the boundaries where binary-search code most often breaks? (Select three.)
options: An empty list, and a one-element list.
Values of `x` smaller than every element and larger than every element.
A list with several copies of `x`.
A single large random list of 10 million distinct values, checked once.
questions.explanation: Off-by-one bugs in binary search appear at the edges: empty and tiny ranges, results at position 0 or len(a), and runs of equal keys where the first match must be found. One large random test rarely hits those boundaries and is slower to debug.
rationales: Correct. Empty and single-element ranges exercise the loop's start and exit conditions.
Correct. These force the answers 0 and len(a).
Correct. Duplicates test that the first qualifying index is returned.

questions.explanation: A subarray (j, i] sums to k exactly when P[i] - P[j] = k, so counting earlier prefixes equal to P[i] - k gives the answer in O(n) expected time. A shrinking window needs the sum to be monotone as the window grows, which negative values break.
rationales: With negatives, shrinking can be wrong, because adding elements can make a too-large sum smaller.
Correct. O(n) expected and handles negatives.
Sorting destroys contiguity.
It counts correctly but is O(n^2), about 2 x 10^10 subarrays at this size.

questions.scenario: You are designing an in-memory LRU cache for an API gateway. get and put must be O(1), and the least recently used entry is evicted when capacity is exceeded.
questions.stem: Which design meets the requirements?
options: A dict alone, relying on insertion order and popping the first key on eviction, without reordering on get.
A Python list of (key, value) pairs; on access, remove the pair and append it to the end.
A min-heap keyed by last-access timestamp, plus a dict for lookups.
A hash map from key to node, plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency (or collections.OrderedDict, which combines both).
questions.explanation: The hash map finds the node in O(1), and the doubly linked list can unlink and relink it, or drop the tail, in O(1). OrderedDict provides the same operations through move_to_end and popitem(last=False).
rationales: Without reordering on get, this is FIFO eviction, not LRU.
Finding and removing a pair in a list is O(n).
Heap updates are O(log n), and timestamp changes leave stale entries.
Correct. The classic O(1) LRU design.

questions.stem: Which two expressions remove duplicates from a list of email strings while keeping the order of first occurrence? (Select two.)
options: list(dict.fromkeys(emails))
list(set(emails))
A loop that appends an email to a result list only if it is not in a seen set, then adds it to seen
sorted(set(emails))
questions.explanation: Dicts preserve insertion order as a language guarantee, so dict.fromkeys keeps first occurrences in order. A seen-set loop does the same explicitly. Set iteration order is not guaranteed, and sorting imposes alphabetical order instead.
rationales: Correct. Insertion-ordered keys, duplicates dropped.
Set order is arbitrary and, for strings, varies between runs because of hash randomization.
Correct. O(n) expected and order-preserving.
Deduplicates but sorts alphabetically, losing the original order.

sources.title: Time complexity of built-in types — Python docs

questions.stem: What does `Counter('abracadabra').most_common(3)` return?
questions.explanation: a appears 5 times, b and r twice each. most_common orders equal counts in the order first encountered, and b appears before r in the string.
rationales: r (2) outranks c (1).
r (2) outranks d (1).
Correct. b is encountered before r.
Ties are not ordered by reverse appearance or alphabetically descending.

questions.stem: You implement an LRU cache on collections.OrderedDict, keeping the most recently used key at the end. Which two calls are correct? (Select two.)
options: On every get or put of an existing key: data.move_to_end(key)
On eviction: data.popitem(last=False)
On eviction: data.popitem()
On every get: data.move_to_end(key, last=False)
questions.explanation: move_to_end(key) marks the key as most recent by moving it to the end. popitem(last=False) removes from the front, which holds the least recently used key. This matches the LRU recipe in the collections docs.
rationales: Correct. Accesses move keys to the most-recent end.
Correct. The front is the least recently used entry.
popitem() defaults to last=True and would evict the most recent entry.
That moves accessed keys to the front, which is where eviction happens.

questions.scenario: A word counter uses `counts = defaultdict(int)`. A later report loops over a list of 10,000 query words and runs `if counts[w]: hits += 1`. Afterwards, `len(counts)` is much larger than the number of distinct words in the corpus.
questions.stem: What is happening, and what is the fix?
options: `counts[w]` calls the default factory for missing keys and inserts them with value 0; use `counts.get(w)` or `w in counts` for read-only checks.
defaultdict duplicates keys when they are read twice; call dict(counts) first.
The hash table never shrinks, so len reports the capacity rather than the item count.
int is the wrong factory; defaultdict(lambda: None) avoids insertion.
questions.explanation: default_factory is called only from __getitem__, and the resulting value is stored under the missing key. get and the in operator do not insert, so they are the right tools for checks that should not modify the mapping.
rationales: Correct. Reads with brackets insert missing keys.
Keys are never duplicated in a dict.
len reports the number of items, not the table capacity.
Any factory still inserts on bracket access; only the stored value changes.

questions.scenario: A path-cost function `cost(path)` is decorated with `@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=None)`. Calling it with `cost([0, 3, 7])` raises `TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'`.
questions.stem: What is the best fix?
options: Set maxsize=128 so the cache uses a list instead of a dict.
Pass a tuple, for example `cost(tuple(path))`, because cached arguments are used as dictionary keys and must be hashable.
Replace lru_cache with functools.cache, which accepts lists.
Convert the list to a string with str(path) inside the function.
questions.explanation: The functools docs state that arguments to an lru_cache-decorated function must be hashable, because the cache is a dictionary keyed by the arguments. Tuples of hashable items are hashable; lists are not.
rationales: maxsize changes eviction, not the key requirement.
Correct. Make the argument hashable at the call boundary.
functools.cache is lru_cache(maxsize=None) and has the same requirement.
The error happens before the function body runs, when the cache builds its key.

questions.scenario: A BST holds the keys 8, 3, 1, 6, 4, 7, 10, 14, 13, inserted in that order. A teammate wants to delete the tree bottom-up so that every node is processed only after both of its children.
questions.stem: Which sequence does that traversal produce?
questions.explanation: Processing children before the parent is postorder (left, right, node). For this tree that gives 1, 4, 7, 6, 3 for the left subtree, then 13, 14, 10 for the right, then the root 8.
rationales: This is inorder, which is sorted for a BST but visits 3 before its descendants 4, 6 and 7.
Correct. Postorder visits both subtrees before each node.
This is level order (breadth-first).
This is preorder (node first), which matches the insertion order here.

questions.scenario: A service builds an unbalanced BST from user ids that arrive in increasing order, then calls a recursive height() function. With 50,000 users it crashes with RecursionError.
questions.stem: What is the best fix that keeps the tree but makes height() reliable?
options: Rewrite height() iteratively, for example a level-order loop over a deque that counts levels, and consider a balanced tree to avoid the chain shape.
Wrap the call in try/except RecursionError and return the recursion limit as the height.
Memoize height() with functools.cache so each node is computed only once.
Raise the limit with sys.setrecursionlimit(10**6) and keep the recursive function.
questions.explanation: Sorted insertion makes the BST a chain of depth about 50,000, far beyond the default limit of 1000. An explicit queue or stack removes the dependence on the call stack, and balancing fixes the underlying O(n) height.
rationales: Correct. Iteration avoids call-stack depth entirely, and balancing removes the degenerate shape.
This returns a wrong value and hides the bug.
Each node is already visited once; memoization does not reduce recursion depth.
A huge limit only treats the symptom: very deep recursion uses a lot of memory, can crash the interpreter on some platforms, and the chain-shaped tree remains.

questions.scenario: A level-order traversal of a tree with about 2 million nodes is much slower than expected. The code uses a Python list as the queue: append() to enqueue and pop(0) to dequeue.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause, and the fix?
options: Level order is inherently O(n log n); switch to inorder traversal.
append() reallocates on every call; preallocate the list with [None] * n.
Python lists are linked lists, so indexing is slow; convert the tree to an array first.
list.pop(0) shifts every remaining element, making the traversal quadratic; use collections.deque and popleft().
questions.explanation: Removing from the front of a list costs time proportional to its length, so n dequeues can cost O(n^2) overall. deque gives O(1) operations at both ends, restoring O(n) traversal.
rationales: Level order visits each node once and is O(n) with a proper queue.
list.append is amortized O(1); preallocation is not the issue.
CPython lists are dynamic arrays with O(1) indexing.
Correct. deque.popleft is O(1).

questions.scenario: A serialisation format stores a binary tree with distinct integer keys as two traversal lists. The team wants the tree to be rebuilt exactly, including whether a single child is a left or right child.
questions.stem: Which pair of traversals should they store?
options: Postorder alone
Preorder and postorder
Preorder and inorder
Level order alone
questions.explanation: With distinct keys, preorder identifies each subtree root and inorder splits its left and right subtrees, so the pair determines the tree uniquely. Preorder plus postorder cannot tell whether a lone child is on the left or the right.
rationales: A single traversal without null markers does not determine the shape.
A node with one child produces the same pre- and postorder whether the child is left or right.
Correct. The root from preorder plus its position in inorder fixes both subtrees.
A single traversal without null markers does not determine the shape.

questions.scenario: A code review finds this BST validator: return true if node.left.val < node.val < node.right.val at every node.
questions.stem: Why is it wrong, and what is the correct approach?
options: It is correct; the BST property is a local parent-child rule.
It misses violations deeper in a subtree, such as a key in the left subtree that is larger than an ancestor; pass min/max bounds down, or check that inorder is strictly increasing.
It must also check that the tree is balanced, since every BST is balanced by definition.
It should compare heights instead of values.
questions.explanation: The BST invariant constrains every key in a subtree relative to each ancestor. A tree with root 10, left child 5 and that child's right child 12 passes the local check but is invalid; bounds or an inorder check catch it.
rationales: The invariant applies to whole subtrees, not just direct children.
Correct. Bounds propagate the ancestor constraints.
BSTs need not be balanced; balance is a separate property.
Heights have nothing to do with key ordering.

questions.scenario: An in-house symbol table uses a plain (unbalanced) BST. Keys are event timestamps that arrive in increasing order. Lookups get slower as the table grows, roughly in proportion to its size.
questions.stem: What explains this, and what is the best remedy?
options: Sorted insertion turns the BST into a chain, so operations cost O(N); use a balanced BST such as a red-black or AVL tree.
The tree needs periodic inorder traversal to stay sorted.
BST lookups are always O(N); only hash tables are faster.
Hash collisions; switch to a better hash function.
questions.explanation: Each new largest key goes to the far right, producing height N - 1. Balanced trees keep height logarithmic regardless of insertion order, so search stays O(log N) in the worst case.
rationales: Correct. Balancing removes dependence on insertion order.
A BST is always in sorted order by its invariant; traversal does not change shape.
With random or balanced shape, BST lookups are logarithmic.
A BST does not hash keys.

questions.stem: Which statements about left-leaning red-black BSTs, as presented in Algorithms 4th ed., are correct? (Select two.)
options: They require a hash function for each key.
They correspond to 2-3 trees, with red links representing 3-nodes.
They guarantee O(1) worst-case search.
Their height is at most 2 lg N.
questions.explanation: A left-leaning red-black BST encodes a 2-3 tree, using a left-leaning red link to join the two keys of a 3-node. Perfect black balance limits height to at most 2 lg N, giving logarithmic worst-case operations.
rationales: Red-black trees are comparison-based, not hash-based.
Correct. That is how the book derives them.
Search is logarithmic, not constant.
Correct. This is the stated height bound.

questions.stem: In an AVL tree, what condition is maintained at every node, and how are violations repaired?
options: The left child is always smaller than the parent; violations are repaired by swapping values with the parent.
Every node is red or black; violations are repaired by rehashing.
The heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most 1; violations are repaired by one or two rotations along the update path.
Every leaf has the same depth; violations are repaired by splitting nodes.
questions.explanation: AVL trees keep each node's balance factor in {-1, 0, +1}. After an insert or delete, heights on the changed path are updated, and any out-of-balance node is fixed with single or double rotations, which are O(1) and preserve inorder order.
rationales: Swapping with the parent describes heap sift operations.
Colours belong to red-black trees, and BSTs do not rehash.
Correct.
Equal leaf depth describes 2-3 or B-trees, not AVL.

questions.scenario: A pricing service must answer: "what is the largest configured price tier less than or equal to x?" Tiers change rarely, and lookups happen thousands of times per second. The tiers are [3, 8, 15, 21].
questions.stem: Using Python's standard library, which approach is best, and what does it return for x = 16?
options: A set with a membership test; returns 16.
A sorted list with i = bisect_right(tiers, x) and tiers[i - 1] when i > 0; returns 15.
A heap with heapq.nsmallest(1, tiers); returns 3.
A dict mapping each tier to itself with dict.get(x); returns None.
questions.explanation: bisect_right returns the insertion point after all elements <= x, so the element before it is the floor. For x = 16 the insertion point is 3 and tiers[2] is 15. With rare updates, the O(n) insert cost of a sorted list does not matter.
rationales: Sets answer exact membership only; 16 is not a tier.
Correct. O(log n) floor query.
A heap gives only the minimum, not a floor.
Hash lookup finds exact keys only.

questions.stem: A workload needs a key-value map that also answers range queries ("all keys between lo and hi in order") and rank queries. Which operations does a balanced BST support in O(log n) worst case that a hash table cannot do efficiently? (Select two.)
options: Ceiling: the smallest key >= x
Exact-key lookup
Rank: the number of keys less than x
Inserting a new key
questions.explanation: Ordered operations such as floor, ceiling, rank and select follow one root-to-leaf path in a balanced BST. A hash table scatters keys, so these require scanning everything; exact lookup and insertion are fast in both structures.
rationales: Correct. Ceiling needs key order.
Hash tables handle exact lookup in O(1) average.
Correct. Rank needs order (and subtree sizes).
Hash tables also insert efficiently, O(1) average.

questions.stem:
On Python 3.13, what does this print?

```python
import heapq
a = [5, 3, 8, 1, 9, 2]
heapq.heapify(a)
print(a)
```
questions.explanation: heapify rearranges the list in place so that heap[k] <= heap[2k+1] and heap[k] <= heap[2k+2]. The result is [1, 3, 2, 5, 9, 8], which satisfies the invariant but is not sorted.
rationales: heapq builds a min-heap, not a max-heap.
Index 2 (8) is larger than its child at index 5 (2), so this violates the invariant.
A heap is not a sorted list; heapify does not sort.
Correct. Sifting down from the last internal node produces this layout.

questions.scenario: A log processor must report the 100 slowest requests out of about 500 million records streamed from disk. Memory is limited to a few hundred MB.
questions.stem: Which approach is best?
options: Insert every record into a dict keyed by latency and take max() 100 times.
Load all records into a list, sort descending and take the first 100.
Keep a min-heap of size 100; for each record, if it is slower than heap[0], call heapreplace. Total O(n log k) time and O(k) memory.
Push all records onto a max-heap (negated) and pop 100 times.
questions.explanation: A size-k min-heap keeps the current top k with the smallest of them at the root, so each record costs at most O(log k). heapq.nlargest(100, stream) implements the same idea. Approaches that hold all n records exceed the memory budget.
rationales: This stores everything and each max() is O(n).
Holding and sorting 500 million records needs far more memory and O(n log n) time.
Correct. Bounded memory and O(n log k) time.
This still stores every record, O(n) memory.

questions.scenario: A developer copies a running-median example from the current Python docs that calls heapq.heappush_max. On the team's Python 3.13 runtime it fails with AttributeError.
questions.stem: What is the right fix?
options: Upgrade nothing; call heapq._heappush_max, which is the public 3.13 name.
Keep a min-heap of negated values: heappush(h, -x) and use -h[0] or -heappop(h).
Pass reverse=True to heapq.heappush.
Use heapq.nlargest(1, h) on every step.
questions.explanation: The public *_max heap functions were added in Python 3.14, so they do not exist on 3.13. Negating keys turns heapq's min-heap into a max-heap at the same O(log n) cost.
rationales: Underscore names are private implementation details, and there is no private push-max function in 3.13 anyway.
Correct. Negation is the standard pre-3.14 technique.
heappush has no reverse parameter.
nlargest scans the whole list, O(n) per step.

questions.scenario: A job scheduler pushes (priority, job) tuples onto a heapq heap, where job is a dict. It works in testing, but in production it occasionally raises TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'dict' and 'dict'.
questions.stem: What is the cause and the recommended fix?
options: Two jobs had equal priority, so tuple comparison fell through to the dicts; push (priority, next(counter), job) using itertools.count().
The heap was not heapified first; call heapify before every push.
dicts are mutable; convert the job to a frozenset.
heapq cannot store tuples; store only the priority.
questions.explanation: Tuples compare element by element, so a tie on priority compares the jobs, and dicts do not support <. The heapq docs recommend an increasing counter as a tie-breaker, which also makes equal priorities pop in insertion order.
rationales: Correct. The counter is never equal for two entries, so jobs are never compared.
heappush maintains the invariant on its own.
frozensets compare by subset, which gives no consistent order and loses the data structure.
Tuples work fine as heap entries.

questions.stem: Which statements about heapq costs are correct? (Select two.)
options: heappop runs in O(1) time because the minimum is at index 0.
Building a heap with n separate heappush calls costs O(n log n) in the worst case.
Iterating over the heap list yields items in sorted order.
heapify on a list of n items runs in O(n) time.
questions.explanation: Bottom-up heapify is linear because most nodes sit near the bottom and sift only a short distance. Each push is O(log n), so n pushes total O(n log n); popping also costs O(log n) because the heap must be restored.
rationales: Reading heap[0] is O(1), but removing it requires a sift-down, O(log n).
Correct.
Only heap[0] is guaranteed to be the minimum; the list is not sorted.
Correct. The heapq docs state heapify is linear time.

questions.scenario: An external sort has written 64 sorted run files totalling 200 GB. The final step must produce one sorted output while reading the runs sequentially.
questions.stem: Which approach fits best?
options: Use bisect.insort to insert every line into an output list.
Concatenate the runs and call sorted() on the result.
Use heapq.merge over 64 file iterators, which lazily holds one item per run and costs O(N log k).
Merge the runs pairwise into one big in-memory list.
questions.explanation: heapq.merge takes already sorted iterables and yields a merged stream lazily, using a heap with one entry per input. With k = 64 runs and N lines this is O(N log k) time and O(k) memory beyond the output.
rationales: Each insort is O(n), giving quadratic time and full memory use.
This loads 200 GB into memory and ignores the existing order.
Correct. A k-way merge is designed for exactly this.
An in-memory list of 200 GB does not fit.

questions.stem:
On Python 3.13, what does this print?

```python
import heapq
h = [1, 5, 3]
heapq.heapify(h)
print(heapq.heapreplace(h, 0), heapq.heappushpop(h, 0))
```
questions.explanation: heapreplace pops first and then pushes, so it returns the old minimum 1 even though 0 is smaller, leaving [0, 5, 3]. heappushpop pushes first and then pops, so with 0 already at the root it returns 0 and the heap is unchanged.
rationales: heapreplace never returns the item it is pushing; it returns the old root.
Correct.
After heapreplace, 0 is in the heap, so heappushpop(h, 0) returns 0.
heapreplace returns 1, the root before the push.

questions.scenario: A Dijkstra implementation needs to lower the priority of a vertex already in a heapq heap. heapq has no decrease-key operation.
questions.stem: What is the standard Python approach?
options: Push a new (distance, vertex) entry and, when popping, skip entries whose distance is larger than the best recorded distance (lazy deletion).
Call heapify after every update to restore order.
Use a sorted list and re-sort after every update.
Search the heap list for the entry, change its priority, and continue without re-heapifying.
questions.explanation: The heapq docs describe marking or ignoring stale entries instead of removing them. Pushing duplicates and skipping stale pops keeps each operation O(log n); the heap may hold O(E) entries.
rationales: Correct. This is lazy deletion.
heapify is O(n) per update, which is far too slow.
Re-sorting is O(n log n) per update.
Editing an entry in place breaks the heap invariant.

questions.scenario: An autocomplete box must return all dictionary words starting with the typed prefix. The dictionary has 2 million words and is updated occasionally. The current code loops over every word and calls startswith().
questions.stem: Which structure most directly reduces the cost to "length of the prefix plus the number of matches"?
options: A min-heap of words
A dict from each word to its length
A set of words
A trie: walk the prefix in O(L), then enumerate the subtree below that node.
questions.explanation: A trie stores shared prefixes once along root-to-node paths. Reaching the prefix node takes O(L) regardless of dictionary size, and every word below it matches, so no non-matching word is examined.
rationales: A heap only gives the smallest item quickly.
Hash maps do not group keys by prefix.
Sets answer exact membership but still require scanning for prefixes.
Correct. Prefix matching is the trie's core strength.

questions.scenario: A trie implementation inserts "cart" and "care". A test calls contains("car") and it returns True, although "car" was never inserted.
questions.stem: What is the most likely bug?
options: Insertion should reverse the word first.
The trie should be stored as a sorted list instead.
contains() returns True when the character path exists, without checking an end-of-word marker on the final node.
The alphabet is too small; use a 256-way array.
questions.explanation: A path in a trie can be a prefix of longer keys. Each node that ends a key must carry a marker (or value), and search must check it at the last character.
rationales: Reversing gives a suffix trie, a different structure.
Changing structure is not needed; the trie only lacks a marker check.
Correct.
Alphabet size affects memory, not this logic.

questions.scenario: A trie for Unicode usernames uses a fixed array of 65,536 child slots in every node. Memory use is enormous even though most nodes have one or two children.
questions.stem: Which change addresses the problem while keeping prefix search?
options: Keep the arrays but use a smaller integer type for each slot.
Store only the children that exist, for example a dict per node or a ternary search trie.
Replace the trie with a hash set of usernames.
Store each username as a separate root.
questions.explanation: An R-way trie spends R links per node, which is wasteful for large alphabets with sparse branching. Sparse child maps or a TST store only the links that exist and still support prefix matching.
rationales: Each node still allocates 65,536 slots, so memory remains huge.
Correct. Algorithms 4th ed. presents TSTs as the space-efficient alternative to R-way tries.
A hash set loses efficient prefix search.
This removes all prefix sharing, the point of a trie.

questions.stem: A static, sorted list words = ['car', 'carbon', 'care', 'cart', 'cat', 'dog'] must answer prefix queries without building a trie. For prefix 'car', which method returns all matches efficiently?
options: i = bisect_left(words, 'car'), then scan forward while words[i].startswith('car'); returns ['car', 'carbon', 'care', 'cart'].
bisect_right(words, 'car'), then scan backward.
Convert words to a set and check 'car' in words.
words.index('car') and return that one word.
questions.explanation: In sorted order, all strings with a given prefix form one contiguous block that starts at the prefix's insertion point. bisect_left finds it in O(log n), and the forward scan touches only the matches plus one.
rationales: Correct. O(log n + number of matches).
Words with the prefix come after the insertion point, not before.
A set gives exact membership only.
This returns only the exact word.

questions.scenario: A network monitor receives a stream of "link a-b came up" events for 10 million hosts and must answer "are hosts x and y connected?" between events. Links never go down.
questions.stem: Which structure and variant should be used?
options: Quick-find union-find, because find is O(1).
A balanced BST of host ids.
Run BFS from x for each query.
Union-find with union by size (or rank) and path compression.
questions.explanation: Union-find handles incremental connectivity directly. With weighted union and path compression, the amortized cost per operation is bounded by the inverse Ackermann function, effectively constant for any practical n.
rationales: Quick-find unions scan the whole array, O(n) per union.
Ordering host ids says nothing about connectivity.
BFS is O(V + E) per query, far too slow for repeated queries.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which statements about union-find (Algorithms 4th ed., section 1.5) are correct? (Select two.)
options: Adding path compression to weighted quick-union makes the amortized cost nearly constant (inverse Ackermann).
Union-find efficiently supports splitting a set back into its original parts.
Weighted quick-union keeps every node's depth at most lg n.
Plain quick-union guarantees O(log n) find in the worst case.
questions.explanation: Linking the smaller tree under the larger means a node's depth grows only when its tree at least doubles, so depth is at most lg n. Path compression on top of that yields inverse-Ackermann amortized cost.
rationales: Correct.
Union-find supports merging only; splitting is not supported efficiently.
Correct.
Plain quick-union can build a chain, making find O(n).

questions.scenario: A dashboard stores per-minute counts for one day (1,440 entries). Counts are updated constantly as late events arrive, and users query arbitrary minute ranges for sums. The current code rebuilds a prefix-sum array after every update.
questions.stem: What is the best replacement?
options: Keep the prefix sums; O(1) queries make them optimal for this workload.
A Fenwick (binary indexed) tree: point update and prefix sum in O(log n), range sum as prefix(r) - prefix(l - 1).
Sum the raw array slice for each query.
A heap of counts.
questions.explanation: Prefix sums give O(1) queries but O(n) per update, which dominates in an update-heavy workload. A Fenwick tree makes both operations O(log n), and sums are invertible, so range sums follow from two prefix queries.
rationales: Each rebuild is O(n), and updates arrive constantly here, so update cost dominates.
Correct.
Each query becomes O(range length).
A heap gives the minimum, not range sums.

questions.scenario: A trading system needs "minimum price between positions l and r" over an array of 10^6 prices, with frequent single-position price updates.
questions.stem: Which structure is the standard fit?
options: A segment tree storing the minimum of each node's range: O(log n) point update and range-min query.
A prefix-minimum array rebuilt after each update.
A single min-heap of all prices.
A Fenwick tree storing prices, querying prefix(r) - prefix(l - 1).
questions.explanation: Range minimum is associative but not invertible, so you cannot get min(l..r) by subtracting prefix results. A segment tree combines O(log n) fully covered nodes for any associative operation and updates O(log n) ancestors.
rationales: Correct.
Prefix minima cannot answer arbitrary ranges, and rebuilding is O(n).
A heap gives the global minimum, not the minimum of a range.
Subtraction does not apply to min; this computes a meaningless difference.

questions.stem: In a 1-based Fenwick tree, entry t[i] stores the sum of the block of length i & -i ending at i. Which index range does t[12] cover?
questions.explanation: 12 is 1100 in binary, so its lowest set bit is 4 (12 & -12 == 4). t[12] therefore covers the 4 positions ending at 12, which are 9 through 12.
rationales: A single-element block applies to odd indices, whose lowest set bit is 1.
That would be a block of length 8.
That would require the block length to be 12.
Correct.

questions.scenario: A report lists orders grouped by region, and within each region the orders must stay in date order. The orders are currently sorted by date. A developer must now sort them by region.
questions.stem: Which approach produces the required order with the least work?
options: Call `orders.sort(key=lambda o: o.region)`; the stable sort keeps date order within each region.
Sort by region with `heapq`-based heapsort, then re-sort each region's slice by date.
Sort by region, then sort again by date so date becomes the tie-breaker.
Write a custom quicksort that partitions on region, since it is faster than the built-in sort.
questions.explanation: Python's sort is guaranteed stable, so records with equal regions keep their existing date order. Since the data is already date-sorted, one sort by region is enough. Sorting by date last would make date the primary key.
rationales: Correct. The secondary order (date) is already in place, and a stable sort by the primary key preserves it.
Heapsort is not stable, which is why the extra per-region pass would be needed. That is more work than one stable sort.
The last sort becomes the primary key, so this orders by date globally and breaks the grouping by region.
A typical quicksort is not stable, so it can scramble date order within a region, and a Python-level quicksort is slower than the built-in C sort.

questions.stem: A vendor claims its new general-purpose comparison sort runs in O(n) time in the worst case for any input of distinct keys. What is the best response?
options: Plausible if it uses a good pivot rule, since median-of-medians gives linear time.
Impossible: any comparison sort needs at least lg(n!) = Θ(n log n) compares in the worst case.
Plausible, because Timsort already does O(n) work on every input.
Impossible, but only because the input must be copied, which costs O(n log n).
questions.explanation: A comparison sort corresponds to a binary decision tree with at least n! leaves, so its height is at least lg(n!) = Θ(n log n). Linear-time sorting requires non-comparison methods and assumptions about key structure, as in counting or radix sort.
rationales: Median of medians selects one order statistic in linear time; it does not sort in linear time.
Correct. This is the decision-tree lower bound, and it is why mergesort is asymptotically optimal.
Timsort is O(n) only on already-ordered runs such as sorted input. Its worst case is O(n log n).
Copying costs O(n), not O(n log n). The real limit is the information-theoretic bound on comparisons.

questions.scenario: A service implements quicksort with the first element as the pivot. Latency is fine in tests with random data, but production calls with already sorted lists of 50,000 items are extremely slow and sometimes hit RecursionError.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Switch to the last element as the pivot.
Raise the recursion limit with `sys.setrecursionlimit` and keep the pivot rule.
Shuffle the input (or choose a random pivot) before partitioning.
Reduce the insertion-sort cutoff to 1.
questions.explanation: A first-element pivot on sorted input produces maximally unbalanced partitions, giving about N²/2 compares and recursion depth n. Randomizing the pivot makes the expected cost O(n log n) for every input, which algs4 recommends.
rationales: Last-element pivots fail the same way on sorted and reverse-sorted input.
This hides the crash but leaves the quadratic running time in place.
Correct. Randomization removes the dependence on input order and keeps the expected recursion depth logarithmic.
The cutoff affects small subarrays only and does nothing about unbalanced partitions.

questions.scenario: You must sort 20 million log records by HTTP status code. There are only about a dozen distinct codes. A colleague's textbook 2-way quicksort is far slower than expected.
questions.stem: Which change addresses the root cause in a quicksort-based design?
options: Use 3-way partitioning so keys equal to the pivot are grouped and excluded from further recursion.
Use the median of three elements as the pivot.
Switch from Lomuto to Hoare partitioning but keep 2-way splits.
Sort the records twice to make the result stable.
questions.explanation: With few distinct keys, 2-way partitioning keeps re-processing large blocks of equal keys. 3-way (Dutch national flag) partitioning puts all keys equal to the pivot in the middle and never touches them again, which algs4 describes as entropy-optimal. Counting sort would also work here, but the question asks about a quicksort design.
rationales: Correct. Grouping equal keys reduces the work toward linear when there are few distinct values.
Median of three improves pivot quality for distinct keys but does not deal with massive duplication.
The partition scheme matters less than the 2-way split itself, which still recurses on equal keys.
Sorting twice does not fix performance and quicksort is not made stable by repetition.

questions.stem: Which of these sorts are stable as normally implemented? (Select two.)
options: Mergesort that takes from the left half on ties
Heapsort
Python's built-in `sorted()`
In-place quicksort with random pivots
questions.explanation: Mergesort is stable when the merge prefers the left run on equal keys, and the Python docs guarantee that sorts are stable. Heapsort and in-place quicksort move elements across long distances and can reorder equal keys.
rationales: Correct. Taking from the left on ties preserves the original order of equal keys.
Heapsort is not stable; the heapq docs say this about heapsort built on heapq.
Correct. The Sorting HOWTO states that sorts are guaranteed to be stable.
Partitioning swaps elements past each other, so equal keys can be reordered.

questions.scenario: An embedded analytics job must sort an array of 10 million fixed-size records in place. The device has almost no spare memory, and the job has a hard deadline, so the worst case matters more than the average. Stability is not required.
questions.stem: Which algorithm best fits these constraints?
options: Mergesort
Heapsort
Quicksort with a fixed middle-element pivot
Counting sort on the record bytes
questions.explanation: Heapsort guarantees O(n log n) time in the worst case using O(1) extra space. Mergesort needs extra space proportional to N, and quicksort has a quadratic worst case.
rationales: Mergesort meets the time bound but needs an auxiliary array of size N, which the device cannot afford.
Correct. It is in place with a worst-case O(n log n) guarantee, and stability is not needed.
A fixed pivot rule still has inputs that cause O(n²) behaviour, so the deadline cannot be guaranteed.
Counting sort needs keys in a small integer range and extra arrays; whole records are not small keys.

questions.scenario: A census pipeline must sort 50 million person records by age in years (0 to 120), keeping records with the same age in their input order.
questions.stem: Which approach has the best asymptotic running time?
options: Mergesort, because it is stable and O(n log n).
Quicksort with 3-way partitioning, because it handles duplicates.
Counting sort with 121 buckets, placing records left to right.
Binary-search insertion of each record into a growing sorted list.
questions.explanation: Ages are integers in a small range k = 121, so counting sort runs in O(n + k), which is linear here. Placing records in input order makes it stable. Comparison sorts are bounded below by Θ(n log n).
rationales: Mergesort is stable and gives a correct result, but it is O(n log n); the small key range allows a linear-time method.
3-way quicksort is efficient with duplicates but is not stable.
Correct. O(n + k) with k tiny, and stable when records are placed left to right.
Each insertion into a list is O(n), so this is O(n²) overall.

questions.scenario: An engineer implements LSD radix sort for 8-digit account numbers. Each digit pass uses a fast in-place partition that is not stable. The output is sorted by the leading digit, but numbers with the same leading digit appear in random order.
questions.stem: What is wrong?
options: LSD radix sort must process digits from most significant to least significant.
Each digit pass must be a stable sort so ties keep the order from earlier passes.
The base is too small; base 10 does not work for radix sort.
Radix sort cannot handle keys with leading zeros.
questions.explanation: LSD radix sort relies on each pass being stable: when two keys share the current digit, their order from the earlier, less significant digits must survive. An unstable pass discards that work, so only the last digit processed is reliably sorted.
rationales: LSD (least significant digit first) is the correct order for this variant; MSD is a different algorithm.
Correct. Stability of each pass is the invariant that makes LSD radix sort correct.
Any base works; it only changes the number of passes and the bucket count.
Fixed-width keys with leading zeros are exactly what LSD radix sort handles naturally.

questions.stem: What does `sorted(["b", "A", "a"], key=str.lower)` return in Python?
questions.explanation: Both "A" and "a" have the key "a", so they tie, and the stable sort keeps their input order: "A" before "a". "b" sorts last.
rationales: This would reverse the tied elements, which a stable sort never does.
Correct. The tie is resolved by original order because Python's sort is stable.
"b" has the key "b", which sorts after the key "a" shared by "A" and "a", so it cannot sit between them.
Uppercase "A" is not moved last; with key=str.lower it ties with "a".

questions.scenario: A team sorts 2 million documents with `sorted(docs, key=expensive_score)`, where `expensive_score` takes about 1 ms per call. A reviewer worries the key will be evaluated on every comparison, about n log n times.
questions.stem: Which statement is accurate?
options: The key is called once per comparison, so caching it with `functools.cache` is required.
The key is called exactly once per element, so about 2 million calls are made.
Using `functools.cmp_to_key` would reduce the number of key evaluations.
The key is called twice per element, once for each side of a comparison.
questions.explanation: The Sorting HOWTO states that the key function is called exactly once for each input record. The sort then compares the stored key values, so the cost is n key calls plus O(n log n) cheap comparisons.
rationales: Keys are computed once up front, so memoization adds nothing here.
Correct. This is the documented decorate-sort-undecorate behaviour of key functions.
cmp_to_key wraps a comparator; a comparator that calls expensive_score would run it on every comparison, which is worse.
Python does not recompute keys per comparison.

questions.stem: Given `a = [1, 2, 2, 2, 3]`, what are `bisect_left(a, 2)` and `bisect_right(a, 2)`?
questions.explanation: bisect_left returns the first index whose element is >= 2, which is 1. bisect_right returns the first index whose element is > 2, which is 4. Their difference, 3, is the count of 2s.
rationales: bisect_right points past the last equal element, which is index 4, not 3.
Correct. Lower bound 1 and upper bound 4.
Index 1 already holds 2, so the lower bound is 1.
a[0] = 1 is less than 2, so the lower bound cannot be 0.

questions.scenario: `events` is a list of `(name, timestamp)` tuples sorted by timestamp. A developer writes `i = bisect_left(events, ("probe", 1700), key=lambda e: e[1])` and gets `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'int' and 'tuple'`.
questions.stem: What is the correct call?
options: `bisect_left(events, ("probe", 1700))` without a key
`bisect_left(events, 1700, key=lambda e: e[1])`
`bisect_left([e[1] for e in events], ("probe", 1700))`
`bisect_left(events, ("probe", 1700), key=lambda e: (e[1],))`
questions.explanation: The bisect docs say the key function is applied to the list elements but not to x. So x must already be a key value, here the timestamp 1700. The original call compared an int key with a tuple.
rationales: Without a key, tuples compare by name first, but the list is sorted by timestamp, so the result is meaningless.
Correct. Pass the key value you are searching for.
The list of timestamps holds ints, so comparing them with the tuple x still raises TypeError, and building the list costs O(n) per call.
The key (1700,) is compared with the tuple ("probe", 1700); their first items are an int and a str, so this still raises TypeError.

questions.scenario:
A developer writes this lower-bound search:

```python
lo, hi = 0, len(a)
while lo < hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if a[mid] < x:
        lo = mid
    else:
        hi = mid
```

It hangs on some inputs.
questions.stem: What is the bug, and what is the fix?
options: The loop should be `while lo <= hi`.
When `a[mid] < x`, mid cannot be the answer, so set `lo = mid + 1`; otherwise lo never advances when `hi == lo + 1`.
mid should be computed as `(lo + hi + 1) // 2` and both branches left as they are.
hi should start at `len(a) - 1`.
questions.explanation: With the half-open invariant a[:lo] < x and a[hi:] >= x, an element with a[mid] < x belongs to the left part, so lo must move past it. When hi == lo + 1, mid equals lo, and `lo = mid` makes no progress, so the loop never ends.
rationales: With `hi = mid`, a `<=` condition loops forever once lo == hi.
Correct. Every branch must strictly shrink the interval.
Rounding up lets mid equal hi; at hi == len(a) that indexes past the end, and otherwise hi = mid can stall.
This breaks the half-open invariant and cannot return len(a) when x is larger than every element.

questions.scenario: Packages with weights `w` (in a fixed order) must ship within D days. Each day the ship loads packages in order until the next one would exceed its capacity. You need the minimum capacity. n is up to 10^5 and weights are up to 500.
questions.stem: Which approach is correct and efficient?
options: Try every capacity from max(w) upward, simulating each one, in O(n · sum(w)).
Binary-search capacities in [max(w), sum(w)] with an O(n) greedy feasibility check, for O(n log sum(w)).
Sort w in descending order and assign packages to days greedily.
Use the median weight times n / D as the capacity.
questions.explanation: Feasibility is monotone: if capacity c works, any larger capacity also works. So you can binary-search the answer range, testing each candidate with a linear greedy simulation. Sorting would break the required package order.
rationales: This finds the right answer but can take up to sum(w) simulations, O(n · sum(w)), which is far too slow.
Correct. A monotone predicate plus binary search on the answer.
Packages must ship in their given order, so reordering them solves a different problem.
This is a heuristic estimate with no guarantee of being minimal or even feasible.

questions.scenario: A monitoring tool needs the median latency of 5 million samples once per minute. The current code sorts the full list each time.
questions.stem: Which method finds the median with the best expected time?
options: Quickselect with a random pivot, expected O(n).
Build a heap with heapify and pop n/2 times, O(n log n).
Binary search over the list for the middle value.
Insert each sample with bisect.insort, then read the middle element.
questions.explanation: Quickselect partitions like quicksort but recurses into only the side containing the target index, giving expected linear time. Median of medians makes it worst-case linear. Sorting or popping half a heap costs O(n log n).
rationales: Correct. Selection does not require sorting.
heapify is linear, but n/2 pops at O(log n) each makes this O(n log n).
Binary search needs sorted input, which is the cost you were trying to avoid.
Each insort is O(n) because of the insertion, so building the list is O(n²).

questions.stem: An interviewer asks for an algorithm that finds the k-th smallest element in O(n) time in the worst case, not just on average. Which algorithm meets that requirement?
options: Randomized quickselect
Median-of-medians selection
Heapsort, then index k
Binary search on the unsorted array
questions.explanation: Median of medians chooses a pivot guaranteed to discard a constant fraction of elements, giving T(n) <= T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + O(n) = O(n). MIT 6.046 lecture 2 covers this linear-time median finding. Randomized quickselect is expected O(n) but O(n²) in the worst case.
rationales: Its expected time is linear, but an unlucky pivot sequence gives O(n²).
Correct. Its pivot guarantee yields a worst-case linear bound.
Sorting first costs O(n log n).
Binary search requires sorted data and is not a selection algorithm.

questions.scenario: A leaderboard job reads 10 million scores and must report the 10 highest. Memory is limited.
questions.stem: Which standard-library approach fits best?
options: `sorted(scores, reverse=True)[:10]`
`heapq.nlargest(10, scores)`
`max(scores)` called 10 times, removing the result each time
`bisect.insort` every score into a list and take the last 10
questions.explanation: heapq.nlargest keeps a heap of size k, so it runs in O(n log k) with O(k) extra memory. The heapq docs say nlargest and nsmallest perform best when the number of items requested is small, recommend sorted() when it is large, and min()/max() when only one item is needed.
rationales: This is O(n log n) and builds a second 10-million-element list.
Correct. Small k with bounded memory is exactly what nlargest is for.
Each max and removal is O(n), and removal mutates the input.
Each insort is O(n), giving O(n²) total.

questions.scenario: A loop adds 200,000 incoming IDs one at a time using `bisect.insort(ids, new_id)`, and nothing reads `ids` until all of them have arrived. The step takes far longer than expected.
questions.stem: What explains the slowness, and what is the better approach?
options: bisect is O(n) per search; use a linear scan instead.
Each insort is O(n) because the list insertion shifts elements, so the loop is O(n²); append all IDs and sort once.
insort is not stable, so it re-sorts the list every time.
The key function is evaluated n times per insertion; pass key=None.
questions.explanation: The bisect docs note that insort's O(log n) search is dominated by the O(n) insertion step. Since no one reads the list until the end, appending in O(1) amortized and sorting once in O(n log n) is much faster.
rationales: The search is O(log n); the cost is in the insertion.
Correct. Batch the inserts and sort once.
insort does not re-sort the list; it inserts at one position.
No key function is involved in this call.

sources.title: Time complexity of built-in types — Python docs

questions.stem: A nightly job re-sorts a 5-million-row list that is already sorted except for a few hundred rows appended at the end. Which statements about using Python's `list.sort()` here are true? (Select two.)
options: Timsort finds the long existing run, so the sort does far fewer comparisons than a full n log n sort.
Python's sort degrades to O(n²) on nearly sorted input, like a first-element-pivot quicksort.
The sort is stable, so rows with equal keys keep their existing relative order.
You should shuffle the list first to avoid the worst case.
questions.explanation: Python's sort is an adaptive natural merge sort: it detects runs already present, and the time-complexity docs note it needs only O(n) comparisons on sorted input. The Sorting HOWTO guarantees stability.
rationales: Correct. Existing order is an advantage for an adaptive sort.
That is a quicksort pathology; Timsort is O(n log n) in the worst case.
Correct. Sorts are guaranteed to be stable.
Shuffling would destroy the existing runs and make the sort slower.

sources.title: Time complexity of built-in types — Python docs

questions.stem: Binary search with `bisect_left(a, x, key=f)` returns a correct lower bound only under which conditions? (Select two.)
options: `a` is sorted in ascending order of `f(element)`.
`a` contains no duplicate keys.
`x` is a key value comparable with `f(element)`, not a raw element.
`len(a)` is a power of two.
questions.explanation: bisect assumes the list is sorted by the same ordering it compares with, here the key. Because key is applied to elements but not to x, x must already be a key value. Duplicates are fine: bisect_left returns the leftmost position among equal keys.
rationales: Correct. The monotone order must be the key order.
Duplicates are allowed; bisect_left and bisect_right give the bounds of the equal block.
Correct. The docs say the key is not applied to x.
Binary search works for any length.

questions.scenario: A routing service loads a road network with about 2 million intersections and 5 million road segments. The prototype stores it as a 2D boolean matrix and runs out of memory at start-up. Most queries iterate over the roads leaving one intersection.
questions.stem: Which change best fits this workload?
options: Store a single list of all edges and scan it for each query
Store the matrix as a dict keyed by (u, v) for every pair of intersections
Store an adjacency list (a list or dict of neighbours per intersection)
Keep the matrix but store it as a list of Python lists of bools
questions.explanation: The graph is sparse (E is close to V), so an adjacency list uses O(V + E) space instead of O(V²) and lists the neighbours of a vertex in O(deg). A matrix of any kind needs about 4 × 10¹² cells here.
rationales: An edge list is compact, but each neighbour query becomes an O(E) scan.
Storing every pair is still O(V²) entries, with more overhead per entry.
Correct. O(V + E) space and O(deg) neighbour iteration match a sparse graph and neighbour-scan queries.
Changing the container does not change the O(V²) cell count; it uses even more memory.

questions.scenario: A social app with 50,000 users stores friendships as defaultdict(list). Profiling shows most time is spent in "are u and v friends?" checks, each of which scans u's friend list. The app also needs to list all friends of a user.
questions.stem: Which representation change keeps neighbour listing efficient and makes the friendship check fast?
options: Store friendships as a single set of (u, v) tuples only
Switch to defaultdict(set) so each check is an average O(1) membership test
Switch to a 50,000 × 50,000 adjacency matrix
Sort each friend list and keep using linear scans
questions.explanation: A dict of sets keeps O(deg) iteration over a user's friends and makes "v in nbrs[u]" an average O(1) test. A matrix would also give O(1) checks but costs O(V²) memory and O(V) neighbour listing.
rationales: Pair lookups are O(1), but listing a user's friends now requires scanning every pair.
Correct. Set membership is O(1) on average and iterating a set is O(deg).
O(1) checks, but 2.5 × 10⁹ cells and O(V) time to list friends.
Sorting enables binary search, but the option keeps linear scans, so nothing improves.

questions.scenario: A puzzle game asks for the minimum number of single-letter changes to turn "COLD" into "WARM", where every intermediate word must be in a 20,000-word dictionary.
questions.stem: Which formulation solves this correctly and efficiently?
options: Run DFS from "COLD" and return the first path that reaches "WARM"
Build a minimum spanning tree of the word graph and read off the tree path
Sort the dictionary and binary-search for words between "COLD" and "WARM"
Treat words as vertices joined when they differ in one letter, and run BFS from "COLD"
questions.explanation: Every change costs one step, so this is an unweighted shortest-path problem on an implicit word graph, which BFS solves in O(V + E). DFS finds some path but not necessarily the shortest one.
rationales: DFS can return a long, winding path; the first path found is not guaranteed minimal.
All edges have equal weight, and an MST path is not a shortest path anyway.
Alphabetical order has nothing to do with one-letter adjacency.
Correct. Unweighted edges plus "minimum number of steps" means BFS.
