questions.scenario: A warehouse robot moves on a grid one cell per step (up, down, left, right) and must reach a charging dock in the fewest moves. A developer's recursive DFS returns a path, but it is often far longer than necessary.
questions.stem: What should the developer change?
options: Use DFS but stop after the first 1000 steps
Use BFS from the robot's cell with a deque, recording parents to rebuild the path
Keep DFS but explore neighbours in a random order
Use Dijkstra with a heap because grids are weighted graphs
questions.explanation: Every move costs the same, so BFS visits cells in order of distance and the first time it reaches the dock is via a shortest path. Dijkstra would also be correct but adds a log factor for no benefit when all weights are equal.
rationales: A depth cutoff neither guarantees a shortest path nor fixes the algorithm choice.
Correct. BFS gives fewest-step paths in unweighted graphs in O(V + E).
Random ordering does not make DFS find shortest paths.
Dijkstra works but is unnecessary overhead when every edge weight is 1; the grid is effectively unweighted.

sources.title: Lecture notes (BFS, DFS, shortest paths) — MIT 6.006

questions.scenario: A BFS over a 1-million-vertex graph uses `queue = [start]` and `u = queue.pop(0)`. It takes minutes, while the same algorithm in another language takes a second.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: BFS is inherently O(V²); switch to DFS
The graph should be converted to an adjacency matrix first
list.pop(0) is O(n), making BFS quadratic; use collections.deque and popleft()
Python dicts are slow; store visited flags in a list of strings
questions.explanation: Removing the first element of a list shifts every remaining element, so each dequeue is O(n). collections.deque offers O(1) appends and pops at both ends, which restores O(V + E).
rationales: BFS is O(V + E) with an O(1) queue.
A matrix makes neighbour iteration O(V) and would make things worse for a sparse graph.
Correct. deque.popleft() is O(1); list.pop(0) is O(n).
Dict and set lookups are average O(1); they are not the bottleneck.

questions.scenario: A BFS marks vertices as visited only when they are dequeued: `u = q.popleft(); if u in seen: continue; seen.add(u)` and then appends every neighbour. On a dense graph the queue grows huge.
questions.stem: What is the best fix?
options: Switch the deque to a list so memory is freed sooner
Mark visited only after all neighbours of u are processed
Replace BFS with a priority queue keyed by vertex id
Add a vertex to seen at the moment it is enqueued and skip neighbours already in seen
questions.explanation: Marking on dequeue allows a vertex to be enqueued once per incoming edge, so the queue can hold O(E) entries. Marking on enqueue guarantees each vertex enters the queue at most once and keeps BFS distances correct.
rationales: A list does not reduce duplicates and makes pop(0) O(n).
Marking even later allows even more duplicates.
A priority queue does not address duplicates and is not needed for unweighted BFS.
Correct. Mark on enqueue so each vertex is queued once.

sources.title: Lecture notes (BFS, DFS, shortest paths) — MIT 6.006

questions.scenario: A recursive DFS works on test graphs but crashes with RecursionError on a production graph that contains a chain of 50,000 linked records. The code runs on CPython 3.13 with default settings.
questions.stem: Which fix is most robust?
options: Switch the visited set to a list
Rewrite DFS with an explicit stack (a list with append/pop)
Wrap the recursive call in try/except RecursionError and continue
Use functools.cache on the DFS function
questions.explanation: CPython's default recursion limit is 1000, so recursion depth equal to the chain length fails. An explicit stack keeps the depth in a heap-allocated list and has the same O(V + E) cost; raising the limit is possible but risks crashing the interpreter on very deep inputs.
rationales: A list makes membership checks O(n) and does nothing for depth.
Correct. An iterative DFS is not limited by the recursion limit.
Swallowing the error silently skips most of the graph.
Caching does not reduce recursion depth on a first traversal.

questions.scenario: A network team needs to know how many isolated clusters exist among 100,000 servers given a list of 300,000 undirected links.
questions.stem: Which two approaches compute the number of connected components in roughly linear time? (Select two.)
options: Run Dijkstra from every vertex and count unreachable pairs
Run BFS or DFS from each vertex that is not yet visited and count the starts
Compute a topological sort and count the vertices with in-degree 0
Process every link with union-find (union by size/rank and path compression) and count distinct roots
questions.explanation: Starting a traversal from each unvisited vertex finds one component per start in O(V + E) total. Union-find processes each edge in nearly constant amortized time, and the number of distinct roots at the end is the component count.
rationales: Running Dijkstra V times is far more expensive and only indirectly gives components.
Correct. Each new start discovers exactly one component.
Topological sort applies to directed acyclic graphs, not undirected components.
Correct. Weighted quick-union with path compression is near-linear overall.

questions.scenario: A package manager checks for circular dependencies by running DFS over a directed graph and reporting a cycle whenever it meets a vertex already in the visited set. Users report false "circular dependency" errors for app → {ui, net}, ui → core, net → core.
questions.stem: What is the correct fix?
options: Treat the graph as undirected and report a cycle when a non-parent visited vertex is seen
Remove the visited set so each vertex is explored once per path
Track vertices on the current DFS stack and report a cycle only for an edge to a vertex still on that stack
Run BFS instead of DFS and report a cycle when a visited vertex is seen
questions.explanation: In a directed graph, reaching an already finished vertex (core via net after ui) is not a cycle. Only a back edge to a vertex that is still on the recursion stack (gray in three-color DFS) indicates a directed cycle.
rationales: Ignoring direction turns the diamond into an undirected cycle, which is still a false positive.
Removing visited makes the search exponential on DAGs with shared dependencies and does not detect cycles correctly.
Correct. Three states (unvisited, on stack, finished) separate back edges from cross edges.
BFS with the same "seen before" rule gives the same false positive on the diamond.

questions.scenario: A course planner runs Kahn's algorithm on 40 courses and their prerequisite edges. The output list contains only 34 courses when the queue empties.
questions.stem: What does this tell you?
options: Six courses have no prerequisites and were skipped
Kahn's algorithm needs a second pass to place the remaining courses
The graph is disconnected, which Kahn's algorithm cannot handle
The prerequisite graph contains a directed cycle, so no valid full ordering exists
questions.explanation: Kahn's algorithm outputs every vertex of a DAG. Vertices on or downstream of a cycle never reach in-degree 0, so a short output proves a cycle exists and no topological order exists.
rationales: Courses with no prerequisites have in-degree 0 and are output first.
Rerunning does not help; those vertices will never reach in-degree 0.
Kahn's algorithm handles disconnected DAGs fine by seeding all in-degree-0 vertices.
Correct. Fewer than V outputs means some in-degrees never reached 0 because of a cycle.

sources.title: Lecture notes (BFS, DFS, shortest paths) — MIT 6.006

questions.scenario:
On CPython 3.13 a developer runs:

```python
from graphlib import TopologicalSorter
ts = TopologicalSorter()
ts.add(3, 2, 1)
ts.add(1, 0)
print(list(ts.static_order()))
```
questions.stem: What is printed?
options: It raises CycleError
questions.explanation: add(node, *predecessors) means the predecessors come first: 2 and 1 before 3, and 0 before 1. With this exact insertion order CPython 3.13 prints [2, 0, 1, 3]; the docs note the order may depend on insertion order, so other code should assert constraints rather than one order.
rationales: There is no cycle: 0 → 1 → 3 and 2 → 3.
Correct. This is the order produced for this insertion sequence; it respects every dependency.
This reverses the dependencies: 3 cannot come before its predecessors.
A valid order in principle, but not what graphlib produces for this insertion sequence.

questions.scenario: A build tool uses graphlib.TopologicalSorter and wants to show a friendly message naming the targets involved when the build graph is circular.
questions.stem: Which handling is correct?
options: Catch RecursionError, because graphlib recurses until it overflows on a cycle
Call get_ready() and treat None as a cycle
Catch graphlib.CycleError from prepare() or static_order() and read the cycle from err.args[1]
Check whether static_order() returns an empty list
questions.explanation: The graphlib docs state that prepare() raises CycleError, a ValueError subclass, when a cycle is detected, and that the cycle is available in args[1]. static_order() calls prepare() and so raises it too.
rationales: graphlib detects cycles explicitly and raises CycleError.
get_ready() returns a tuple of ready nodes, and it is only used after prepare() succeeds.
Correct. CycleError carries the detected cycle in args[1].
A cycle raises an exception; it does not return an empty order.

questions.scenario: A student implements DFS-based topological sort by appending each vertex to the result when DFS first visits it (preorder), then returns that list. For edges a → c, b → a, the output is sometimes wrong.
questions.stem: What should the student return instead?
options: The preorder list reversed
The BFS order from the vertex with the most edges
The vertices sorted by out-degree
The reverse of the postorder: append each vertex when its DFS call finishes, then reverse the list
questions.explanation: In a DAG, a vertex finishes only after everything reachable from it has finished, so reverse postorder puts every vertex before its successors. Preorder (reversed or not) breaks when DFS starts from a vertex like a before reaching its predecessor b.
rationales: Reversed preorder is not reliable: depending on where DFS starts it can still place a vertex before one of its predecessors.
BFS order from an arbitrary vertex ignores which vertices are predecessors.
Degree does not encode the ordering constraints.
Correct. Reverse postorder of a DAG is a topological order.

questions.scenario: A CI system has 200 build steps with dependencies and 8 worker machines. It wants to start each step as soon as all its dependencies finish, keeping workers busy.
questions.stem: Which use of graphlib.TopologicalSorter fits?
options: Call prepare(); while is_active(), dispatch every node from get_ready() to workers and call done(node) as each finishes
Call static_order() and run the steps one at a time in that order
Call static_order() and split the list into 8 equal consecutive chunks, one per worker
Call get_ready() once and run only those nodes in parallel
questions.explanation: The prepare/get_ready/done/is_active protocol is designed for parallel processing: get_ready() returns every node whose predecessors are done, and done() unlocks dependants. Splitting a static order into chunks can run a step before its dependency in another chunk finishes.
rationales: Correct. This is the documented pattern for concurrent processing.
Valid but serial; it leaves 7 workers idle.
Chunks run concurrently, so a step can start before a dependency in an earlier chunk completes.
Only the initial wave runs; later steps never become ready without done().

questions.scenario: A currency-exchange model has edge weights that can be negative (rebates). For edges A → B (2), A → C (5) and C → B (−4), a Dijkstra implementation that finalises vertices when they are first popped reports dist(B) = 2.
questions.stem: What is happening, and what should be used?
options: Run BFS, because negative weights cancel out.
Dijkstra assumes nonnegative weights; B was finalised before the cheaper path A → C → B (cost 1) was seen. Use Bellman-Ford.
The heap is corrupted; push (vertex, distance) instead of (distance, vertex).
Add 4 to every edge weight so all are nonnegative and keep Dijkstra.
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's greedy step is only safe when no later edge can lower a finalised distance, which requires nonnegative weights. Bellman-Ford handles negative edges and finds dist(B) = 1 here.
rationales: BFS ignores weights entirely.
Correct. Negative edges break Dijkstra's invariant; Bellman-Ford is correct with negative weights.
Tuple order matters for the heap key, but the error comes from the negative edge, not tuple order.
Adding a constant penalises paths with more edges and can change which path is shortest.

questions.scenario: Dijkstra is written with heapq. When a shorter distance to v is found, the code pushes a new (nd, v) entry without removing the old one.
questions.stem: Which line must the main loop contain for this to be correct and efficient?
options: After popping (d, u), call heapq.heapify(pq) to remove duplicates
Before pushing, search the heap list for v and update its priority in place
Pop until the heap is empty, then re-run the algorithm a second time
After popping (d, u), skip it if d > dist[u]
questions.explanation: This is lazy deletion: outdated entries stay in the heap and are ignored when popped, because their distance no longer matches dist[u]. heapq has no decrease-key, and editing the list in place breaks the heap invariant unless it is re-heapified.
rationales: heapify reorders entries but does not remove duplicates, and costs O(n) per call.
Searching the list is O(n) per update, and changing a priority in place breaks the heap invariant.
A second run is wasteful and not needed with the stale-entry check.
Correct. Skipping stale entries keeps each vertex processed once with its final distance.

questions.scenario: A directed graph has edges A → B (4), A → C (1), C → B (2), B → D (1), C → D (5), D → E (3). All weights are nonnegative.
questions.stem: What is the shortest distance from A to E?
questions.explanation: Dijkstra finalises C at 1, then B at 3 via A → C → B, then D at 4 via B, and E at 7 via D. The path is A → C → B → D → E.
rationales: This is A → C → D → E (1 + 5 + 3).
No path from A to E costs 6.
This is A → B → D → E (4 + 1 + 3), which ignores the cheaper route to B through C.

questions.scenario: A payments graph may contain cycles of trades whose weights sum to a negative number. The team runs Bellman-Ford from one source with V − 1 passes over all edges.
questions.stem: How should they detect whether a negative cycle is reachable from the source?
options: Check whether the graph has more edges than vertices
Run one more pass; if any edge can still be relaxed, a reachable negative cycle exists
Check whether any final distance is negative
Run Dijkstra and compare its distances with Bellman-Ford's
questions.explanation: After V − 1 passes all shortest paths without cycles are settled. If another pass still lowers a distance, some reachable cycle keeps reducing cost, which means it is negative.
rationales: Edge count says nothing about cycle weights.
Correct. An improvement on the V-th pass proves a reachable negative cycle.
Negative distances are normal with negative edges and do not imply a cycle.
Dijkstra is invalid with negative edges, so disagreement proves nothing specific.

sources.title: Lecture notes (BFS, DFS, shortest paths) — MIT 6.006

questions.scenario: A project schedule is a DAG of tasks. Edge weights are durations, and some edges carry negative weights to model overlaps. The planner needs both earliest-start times (shortest paths) and the critical path (longest path) from the start task.
questions.stem: Which approach is correct and most efficient?
options: Run Dijkstra for shortest paths and Dijkstra with negated weights for longest paths
Run Bellman-Ford for both; nothing faster works with negative weights
Run BFS and multiply hop counts by the average duration
Topologically sort the DAG and relax edges in that order (negate weights for the longest path), O(V + E)
questions.explanation: In a DAG, relaxing vertices in topological order finalises each distance when it is reached, in O(V + E), and works with negative weights. Negating the weights (or taking max) gives longest paths, which is how critical paths are computed.
rationales: Dijkstra fails with negative weights, and negating weights creates them.
Bellman-Ford is correct but O(V · E); the DAG structure allows linear time.
BFS ignores the actual durations.
Correct. Topological-order relaxation handles any weights in a DAG in linear time.

questions.scenario: A reviewer is checking a Dijkstra implementation that uses heapq with lazy deletion on a graph with nonnegative weights.
questions.stem: Which two statements about this implementation are correct? (Select two.)
options: The heap can hold O(E) entries because a vertex may be pushed once per improving edge
It handles negative edge weights as long as there is no negative cycle
The running time is O((V + E) log V)
heapq provides a decrease_key function that avoids duplicates
questions.explanation: With lazy deletion every successful relaxation pushes an entry, so the heap may hold O(E) items, and each push or pop costs O(log E) = O(log V). Dijkstra is still restricted to nonnegative weights, and heapq has no decrease-key.
rationales: Correct. One push per improving relaxation gives up to O(E) entries.
Dijkstra needs nonnegative weights even without negative cycles.
Correct. O(E) heap operations at O(log V) each, plus O(V + E) scanning.
heapq has no decrease-key; that is why lazy deletion is used.

questions.scenario: A utility company must connect 6 substations with cable at minimum total cost. Candidate links and costs are known, and all costs are distinct.
questions.stem: How does Kruskal's algorithm decide whether to keep the next-cheapest link?
options: Keep it only if it shortens the path from substation 1 to some other substation
Keep every link whose cost is below the average cost
Keep it unless union-find shows both endpoints are already in the same component
Keep it only if it is adjacent to the tree built so far
questions.explanation: Kruskal considers edges in increasing weight and adds each one that connects two different components, which union-find checks in near-constant time. An edge between vertices already connected would form a cycle.
rationales: Path length from a source is a shortest-path concern, not an MST rule.
A cost threshold ignores cycles and connectivity.
Correct. Edges joining two different components are safe to add by the cut property.
Growing a single connected tree is Prim's algorithm, not Kruskal's.

questions.scenario: An undirected graph has edges A–B (1), B–C (2), A–C (3), C–D (4), B–D (5).
questions.stem: What is the total weight of its minimum spanning tree?
questions.explanation: Kruskal takes A–B (1) and B–C (2), skips A–C (3) because A and C are already connected, then takes C–D (4). The total is 1 + 2 + 4 = 7.
rationales: This includes A–C, which forms a cycle with A–B and B–C.
Correct. Edges A–B, B–C, C–D.
6 is A–B + B–C + A–C, which forms a cycle and leaves D unconnected.
This would use A–C or B–D instead of a cheaper valid edge.

questions.scenario: A logistics team computed an MST over the road network to plan a fibre backbone. A manager now proposes using the same MST to route delivery vans along the cheapest route between depots.
questions.stem: What is the best response?
options: The MST path between two depots is always a shortest path, so it is fine
Recompute the MST with Prim from the source depot; Prim's tree is a shortest-path tree
Use the MST but add the reverse of every edge
The MST minimises total edge weight, not pairwise path length; use a shortest-path algorithm such as Dijkstra for routes
questions.explanation: An MST connects all vertices with the least total weight, but the tree path between two vertices can be much longer than the direct shortest path. Prim resembles Dijkstra but keys on single edge weights, so its tree is still an MST, not a shortest-path tree.
rationales: Counterexample: a triangle with weights 1, 1 and 1.5 has MST path 2 between the endpoints of the 1.5 edge.
Prim produces an MST regardless of the start vertex.
Adding reverse edges to an undirected tree changes nothing about path lengths.
Correct. Routes need shortest paths; the backbone needs an MST.

questions.scenario: An analyst is preparing an MST computation and wonders how changes to the input affect the result.
questions.stem: Which two statements are true? (Select two.)
options: Adding the same constant to every edge weight can change which edges are in the MST
An MST of a graph with V vertices can have fewer than V − 1 edges when the graph is connected
Kruskal and Prim work correctly with negative edge weights
If the graph is disconnected, the algorithms produce a minimum spanning forest, one tree per component
questions.explanation: MST algorithms only compare edge weights, so negative or zero weights are fine, and on a disconnected graph they yield a spanning forest. Every spanning tree has exactly V − 1 edges, so adding a constant shifts every tree's total equally and leaves the MST unchanged.
rationales: All spanning trees have V − 1 edges, so a uniform shift preserves their ranking.
A spanning tree of a connected graph has exactly V − 1 edges.
Correct. Only relative order of weights matters to Kruskal and Prim.
Correct. Each component gets its own minimum spanning tree.

questions.scenario: A codebase has 3,000 modules with import edges, including several import cycles. The team wants to group modules that are mutually dependent and then order the groups for a staged refactor.
questions.stem: Which approach fits?
options: Compute an MST of the import graph and order modules by tree depth
Run BFS from the main module and group modules by distance
Compute strongly connected components (for example with Kosaraju-Sharir), collapse each into one node, and topologically sort the resulting DAG
Run Kahn's algorithm directly; it will order modules inside cycles arbitrarily
questions.explanation: Each SCC is a maximal group of modules that can all reach each other, which is exactly a set of mutually dependent modules. The condensation graph of SCCs is always a DAG, so it can then be topologically sorted.
rationales: MSTs are for undirected weighted graphs and say nothing about dependency order.
BFS distance does not identify mutual reachability.
Correct. SCCs find mutual-dependency groups, and the condensation is a DAG.
Kahn's algorithm stalls on cycles; vertices on a cycle never reach in-degree 0.

questions.scenario: A developer implements Kosaraju-Sharir. Step 1 runs DFS on the reversed graph and records reverse postorder. Step 2 runs DFS on the original graph, but starts each new search from vertices in increasing id order. Some reported SCCs contain vertices that cannot reach each other.
questions.stem: What is the fix?
options: Skip step 1 and run a single DFS on the original graph
In step 2, start new searches in the reverse postorder computed in step 1
Run step 2 on the reversed graph as well
Use BFS in step 2 instead of DFS
questions.explanation: The algorithm's correctness depends on step 2 visiting vertices in the reverse postorder of the reversed graph, which ensures each search starts in a "sink" component and cannot leak into other components. Any other start order can merge several SCCs into one tree.
rationales: A single plain DFS cannot separate SCCs without extra bookkeeping such as Tarjan's low-links.
Correct. The step-1 order is what keeps each step-2 tree inside one SCC.
Running both passes on the same graph loses the property the algorithm relies on.
The traversal type is not the issue; the start order is.

questions.scenario: A developer adds @functools.cache to a recursive mergesort helper that sorts the left and right halves of a list slice, hoping to speed it up. Benchmarks show no improvement.
questions.stem: Why did memoization not help?
options: Mergesort's subproblems do not overlap, so each one is computed once and the cache never produces a useful hit.
The cache was too small; lru_cache with a larger maxsize would fix it.
Mergesort lacks optimal substructure, so DP cannot be applied.
functools.cache only works on functions with integer arguments.
questions.explanation: Memoization pays off only when the same subproblem is requested more than once. Mergesort's recursion splits into disjoint halves, so there is nothing to reuse. It does have optimal substructure, so that is not the reason.
rationales: Correct. Without overlapping subproblems, caching adds overhead and no reuse.
functools.cache is already unbounded; size is not the issue.
Sorted halves combine into a sorted whole, which is substructure; the missing property is overlap.
functools.cache accepts any hashable arguments, not just integers.

questions.scenario: A memoized recursive solution with @functools.cache passes all unit tests with n ≤ 500. In production, inputs with n = 20,000 crash with RecursionError.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Switch @cache to @lru_cache(maxsize=128) to reduce memory pressure.
Wrap the call in try/except RecursionError and return 0.
Rewrite the recurrence bottom-up as a loop over subproblems in topological order.
Replace the cache with a global dict; dicts do not count toward recursion depth.
questions.explanation: The recursion depth grows with n and Python's default recursion limit is 1000. A bottom-up tabulation computes the same subproblems in a loop with no call stack growth. Changing the cache type does not change recursion depth.
rationales: A bounded cache causes recomputation and does nothing about depth.
Swallowing the error returns wrong answers.
Correct. Tabulation removes the deep call stack entirely.
How results are stored is irrelevant; the recursive calls themselves create the depth.

questions.scenario: For 'maximise stock-trading profit with at most one share held at a time and a one-day cooldown after each sale', a teammate defines dp[i] = best profit achievable by the end of day i and writes a recurrence over i alone. It gives wrong answers on some tests.
questions.stem: What is the most likely flaw in the design?
options: dp[i] should be replaced with a greedy rule that sells at every local maximum.
The state omits information the future depends on (whether a share is currently held, or a cooldown is active), so histories needing different continuations collapse into one state.
The DP should be top-down instead of bottom-up.
The prices should be sorted before running the DP.
questions.explanation: A correct state must capture everything that affects the remaining decisions. Whether you hold a share or are in cooldown changes which actions are legal tomorrow, so the day index alone merges incompatible histories. Add a small holding or cooldown flag to the state.
rationales: Selling at every local maximum ignores the cooldown and is not optimal in general.
Correct. The state is under-specified for the constraints.
Top-down and bottom-up compute the same recurrence; evaluation order does not fix a wrong state.
Sorting prices destroys the time order the problem is about.

questions.stem: Which statements about memoization versus tabulation are accurate? (Select two.)
options: Tabulation makes it easy to keep only the last row or two of the table to reduce space.
Memoization requires choosing a topological order explicitly.
Memoization may compute only the subproblems actually reachable from the original problem.
Tabulation always uses less time than memoization for the same recurrence.
questions.explanation: Top-down memoization lets the recursion discover which subproblems are needed, possibly skipping some. Bottom-up tabulation requires you to pick the order, which in turn makes rolling-array space savings straightforward. Asymptotic time is usually the same.
rationales: Correct. Knowing the fill order lets you discard rows that will never be read again.
That is tabulation; memoization gets the order implicitly from recursion.
Correct. Only subproblems on recursion paths are computed.
Both evaluate the same recurrence; tabulation may even compute unneeded entries.

questions.scenario: A DP for a string problem has subproblems x(i, j) for 0 ≤ i ≤ j < n and each subproblem takes the minimum over all k with i ≤ k < j.
questions.stem: What is the running time of the DP?
options: O(n)
questions.explanation: There are O(n^2) (i, j) pairs and each does O(n) work over k. Time is subproblems times work per subproblem, giving O(n^3).
rationales: That counts subproblems but ignores the O(n) work in each.
Correct. O(n^2) × O(n).
Caching removes the exponential blow-up of the naive recursion.
There are quadratically many subproblems, so linear time is impossible.

questions.scenario: A 0/1 knapsack is implemented with a single 1-D array best[0..W]. For each item (w, v) the code runs `for c in range(w, W + 1): best[c] = max(best[c], best[c - w] + v)`. On items (3, 4) and W = 6 it returns 8.
questions.stem: What is wrong?
options: Nothing; 8 is the correct answer.
best must be initialised to negative infinity instead of 0.
The ascending capacity loop lets best[c - w] already include the current item, so an item can be used twice; iterate c from W down to w.
The outer loop should iterate over capacities and the inner loop over items.
questions.explanation: Scanning capacity upwards reads best[c - w] after it was updated with the same item, which is the unbounded-knapsack recurrence. With one item of weight 3 the 0/1 answer for W = 6 is 4, not 8. Descending capacity keeps each item to a single use.
rationales: With a single copy of the item the best value is 4.
Zero initialisation is correct when the capacity need not be filled exactly.
Correct. Descending order preserves the previous row's values.
Swapping loops with this update is the unbounded (or combination-counting) variant, not 0/1.

sources.title: Dynamic Programming Part 4 (subset sum, pseudopolynomial) — MIT 6.006 (Spring 2020)

questions.scenario: A reviewer claims: "Our 0/1 knapsack DP runs in O(nW), which is polynomial, so we have shown knapsack is in P."
questions.stem: What is the best response?
options: Correct, but only when all weights are distinct.
Correct, which proves P = NP since knapsack is NP-complete.
Incorrect: O(nW) is pseudopolynomial because W is encoded in about log W bits, so the running time is exponential in the input size.
Incorrect: the DP is actually O(2^n) because each item is either taken or not.
questions.explanation: Input size counts bits, and W needs only about log W bits. A running time linear in the numeric value W is therefore exponential in input length. MIT 6.006 discusses this as pseudopolynomial time, and knapsack remains NP-complete.
rationales: Distinct weights do not change the encoding argument.
The DP is not polynomial in input size, so it proves nothing about P versus NP.
Correct. This is the definition of pseudopolynomial.
The table has n × W entries; the DP avoids enumerating 2^n subsets.

questions.stem: What is the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence of [10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18]?
questions.explanation: One longest strictly increasing subsequence is 2, 3, 7, 18 (or 2, 5, 7, 101). No increasing subsequence of length 5 exists. The O(n log n) tails method also ends with four entries.
rationales: No five elements of the array are in strictly increasing order and position.
The array has only eight elements with several descents; six is impossible.
2, 5, 7 can be extended with 18 or 101.
Correct.

questions.scenario: An engineer uses the O(n log n) LIS method with a `tails` list and bisect_left, then returns `tails` to the caller as "the longest increasing subsequence".
questions.stem: What is the problem with returning tails?
options: tails has the correct length but its elements need not form a subsequence of the input in order; keep predecessor indices to reconstruct one.
bisect_left gives non-decreasing subsequences, so tails may contain duplicates.
tails is always correct; there is no problem.
tails is in decreasing order and must be reversed.
questions.explanation: Each tails[k] is the smallest tail of any increasing subsequence of length k+1, and entries can come from different subsequences. Only len(tails) is guaranteed. To output an actual LIS, store the index of each element's predecessor and walk back.
rationales: Correct. For [3, 4, 1] tails ends as [1, 4], which is not a subsequence in order.
bisect_left replaces equal values, which gives strictly increasing; bisect_right would allow equal values.
The values can be mixed from different candidate subsequences.
tails is kept sorted increasing.

questions.stem: What is the edit distance (insert, delete, substitute, each cost 1) between "kitten" and "sitting"?
questions.explanation: Substitute k→s, substitute e→i, and insert g at the end: three operations. The standard O(mn) DP confirms that no two-operation sequence exists.
rationales: Two differing letters plus a length difference of one need at least three edits.
Correct.
Three operations suffice.
That is the length of "sitting", the cost of building it from scratch.

questions.stem: How many monotone paths (moves only right or down) go from the top-left to the bottom-right cell of a grid with 3 rows and 7 columns?
questions.explanation: A path is a sequence of 2 down moves and 6 right moves, so the count is C(8, 2) = 28. The DP P(i,j) = P(i−1,j) + P(i,j−1) with ones on the first row and column gives the same value.
rationales: That is C(9, 3), treating the grid as larger than it is.
That is C(7, 2), which miscounts the number of moves.
Correct.
That is C(9, 2), one move too many.

questions.scenario: An interval DP for matrix-chain multiplication computes C[i][j] = min over k of C[i][k] + C[k+1][j] + cost. The code fills the table with `for i in range(n): for j in range(i+1, n): ...` and returns wrong values.
questions.stem: What change fixes the fill order?
options: Use memoization with lru_cache(maxsize=1) to save memory.
Sort the matrices by dimension first.
Iterate by increasing interval length (j − i), or with i descending, so C[k+1][j] is ready before C[i][j].
Iterate j descending inside i ascending.
questions.explanation: C[i][j] depends on intervals that start later than i, such as [k+1, j]. With i ascending those rows are still empty. Filling by increasing length (or i from n−1 down) gives a valid topological order.
rationales: A cache of size one would recompute almost everything.
Matrix order is fixed by the product; reordering changes the problem.
Correct. Shorter intervals must be computed first.
C[k+1][j] with larger start index is still uncomputed for every j.

questions.stem: Which problems are naturally solved with an O(mn) two-index DP over prefixes of two sequences? (Select two.)
options: Huffman coding
Edit distance
Interval scheduling
Longest common subsequence
questions.explanation: LCS and edit distance both define a subproblem for every pair of prefixes and combine three neighbouring entries. Huffman coding and unweighted interval scheduling are greedy algorithms.
rationales: Huffman is a greedy heap-based algorithm.
Correct. E(i,j) over prefixes of both strings.
Unweighted interval scheduling is solved greedily by finish time.
Correct. L(i,j) over prefixes of both strings.

sources.title: Dynamic Programming Part 2 (LCS, LIS, coins) — MIT 6.006 (Spring 2020)

questions.scenario: A booking system must accept the maximum number of non-overlapping meeting requests in one room. Each request has a start and end time and all requests are equally valuable.
questions.stem: Which strategy is guaranteed optimal?
options: Sort by start time and accept each compatible request.
Sort by duration, shortest first, and accept each compatible request.
Accept the request with the fewest conflicts, remove its conflicts, and repeat.
Sort by end time and accept each request that starts at or after the last accepted end.
questions.explanation: Earliest finish time is optimal by an exchange argument: the first greedy request ends no later than the first request of any optimal schedule, so it can replace it. The other rules all have counterexamples.
rationales: One early, long meeting can block many short ones.
A short meeting that overlaps two otherwise compatible meetings can reduce the total.
Fewest-conflicts also has known counterexamples.
Correct. This is the classic greedy proven optimal in MIT 6.046.

questions.scenario: The same booking system now assigns each request a revenue value and must maximise total revenue rather than the count of meetings.
questions.stem: What should the team do?
options: Use Huffman coding on the revenue values.
Keep earliest-finish-first; it remains optimal with weights.
Sort by value descending and accept each compatible request.
Use dynamic programming over requests sorted by finish time, choosing for each to take it (plus the best compatible prefix) or skip it.
questions.explanation: With weights, the greedy choice property fails: a single long high-value request can beat several short ones, or the reverse. Weighted interval scheduling is solved by DP with a binary search for the last compatible request, in O(n log n).
rationales: Huffman coding builds prefix codes; it does not schedule intervals.
Earliest finish ignores weights and can lose revenue.
Highest value first can block several requests whose combined value is larger.
Correct. Take-or-skip DP handles weights optimally.

questions.stem: A currency has coins worth 1, 3 and 4. For an amount of 6, how many coins does the 'largest coin first' greedy use, and what is the optimum?
options: Greedy 3, optimum 3
Greedy 4, optimum 2
Greedy 2, optimum 2
Greedy 3, optimum 2
questions.explanation: Greedy takes 4, then 1 and 1, for three coins. Two coins of 3 make 6. Greedy coin change is only safe for special denomination systems; the general problem needs DP.
rationales: 3 + 3 uses only two coins.
Greedy uses 4 + 1 + 1, three coins.
Greedy cannot finish with two coins after taking a 4.
Correct.

sources.title: Dynamic Programming Part 2 (LCS, LIS, coins) — MIT 6.006 (Spring 2020)

questions.stem: Symbols have frequencies 1, 1, 2 and 4. What is the total number of bits in the Huffman encoding (sum of frequency × codeword length)?
questions.explanation: Merge 1+1=2, then 2+2=4, then 4+4=8. The total cost is the sum of merged weights: 2 + 4 + 8 = 14. Equivalently, depths 3, 3, 2, 1 give 3 + 3 + 4 + 4 = 14.
rationales: That is the cost of a fixed-length 2-bit code: 8 occurrences × 2 bits.
Too few; no prefix-free code achieves it for these frequencies.
That is the total frequency, not the bit count.
Correct.

questions.scenario: A Huffman implementation pushes tuples (frequency, node) into heapq, where node is an instance of a small Node class with no ordering methods. It works on most inputs but raises TypeError on some.
questions.stem: What is the cause and fix?
options: heapq requires a max-heap; negate the frequencies.
Two entries with equal frequency make tuple comparison fall through to the Node objects, which are not orderable; push (frequency, counter, node) with a unique counter.
heapq cannot store tuples; store only frequencies in the heap.
Huffman requires frequencies to be sorted before heapify.
questions.explanation: Tuples compare element by element, so equal frequencies lead heapq to compare the nodes with <. The heapq docs recommend a tie-breaking count so that the payload is never compared. heapify handles unsorted input.
rationales: Huffman needs the two smallest frequencies, which is exactly a min-heap.
Correct. A monotonically increasing counter breaks ties.
Tuples are fine in heapq; the payload is the problem.
heapify builds a valid heap from any order in linear time.

questions.stem: Which statements correctly describe how greedy correctness is established or fails? (Select two.)
options: Any problem with optimal substructure can be solved greedily.
An exchange argument transforms an optimal solution into the greedy one step by step without making it worse.
If a greedy algorithm is correct on every hand-made test case, it is proven optimal.
Taking items by highest value/weight ratio is optimal for fractional knapsack but not for 0/1 knapsack.
questions.explanation: Greedy algorithms need a proof such as an exchange argument or 'greedy stays ahead'. Fractional knapsack allows splitting the last item, so ratio order is optimal, while 0/1 knapsack has counterexamples. Optimal substructure alone justifies DP, not greedy.
rationales: Greedy also needs the greedy choice property; 0/1 knapsack has optimal substructure but needs DP.
Correct. This is the standard proof technique.
Testing cannot prove optimality; counterexamples are often subtle.
Correct. Example: capacity 7 with (1,1), (3,4), (4,5), (5,7): ratio-greedy gets 8, the optimum is 9.

questions.scenario: A subsets generator uses backtracking with a shared list `path`. On reaching a leaf it runs `results.append(path)`. For input [1, 2] it returns [[], [], [], []].
questions.stem: What is the bug?
options: results stores references to the same mutable list, which is empty after backtracking finishes; append a copy such as path[:] or tuple(path).
Subsets of [1, 2] should be generated with itertools.permutations.
The un-choose step `path.pop()` should be removed.
The recursion visits leaves in the wrong order.
questions.explanation: Every append stores the same list object, and by the end every choose has been undone. Recording a snapshot fixes it. Removing the pop would corrupt the search instead.
rationales: Correct. Snapshot the path at each leaf.
Permutations give orderings, not subsets.
Without pop, state leaks between branches and results are wrong.
Order would not make entries empty.

questions.stem: A function must list every ordering of 9 distinct tasks. Roughly how many outputs will it produce, and what does that imply?
options: 362,880 (9!); output size alone forces at least that much work, so no algorithm can be polynomial in n for this task.
81 (9^2); a nested loop is enough.
36 (C(9, 2)); use itertools.combinations.
About 512 (2^9); any O(n^2) algorithm suffices.
questions.explanation: There are n! permutations of n distinct items, and 9! = 362,880. When the task is to list them all, the output size is a lower bound on the running time. itertools.permutations produces them lazily.
rationales: Correct.
n^2 counts ordered pairs.
C(9, 2) counts unordered pairs.
2^n counts subsets, not orderings.

questions.scenario: A backtracking search finds subsets of an integer list summing to a target. To speed it up, a developer adds: stop exploring as soon as the partial sum exceeds the target. Some valid answers disappear.
questions.stem: Why?
options: The input contains negative numbers, so a partial sum above the target can still come back down; the prune is only valid for non-negative values.
Backtracking cannot be pruned; it must explore every branch.
The prune should be 'partial sum below target'.
The list must be sorted descending for any pruning to work.
questions.explanation: A pruning rule must never discard a branch that could still lead to a solution. Exceeding the target is a dead end only if all remaining values are non-negative. With negatives, use a bound that accounts for the most negative remaining sum, or no such prune.
rationales: Correct. The prune assumes monotone partial sums.
Pruning is the main tool that makes backtracking practical, when it is sound.
That would discard almost every branch early.
Sorting can help ordering, but it does not make this prune valid with negatives.

questions.stem: Which techniques reduce the work of an N-Queens or Sudoku backtracking solver without changing its answers? (Select two.)
options: Skip the un-choose step to save time.
Track used columns and diagonals in sets so each conflict check is O(1).
Pick the next cell or variable at random to avoid worst cases, and stop after the first random failure.
Choose the most constrained variable (fewest remaining candidates) first so failures appear earlier.
questions.explanation: Constant-time validity checks and most-constrained-first ordering both preserve correctness while cutting work. Stopping after a random failure can miss solutions, and skipping the un-choose step corrupts state.
rationales: Without undoing choices, later branches see stale constraints.
Correct. Keys c, r−c and r+c identify columns and diagonals.
Stopping on the first failure is not exhaustive and can miss solutions.
Correct. Fail-first ordering prunes larger subtrees.

questions.scenario: In an interview you are given an array problem with n up to 2 × 10^5 and a 1-second limit. You immediately see an O(n^2) solution.
questions.stem: What is the best next step?
options: Ask for the constraint to be lowered to n ≤ 1000.
Jump to a backtracking search with pruning.
Code the O(n^2) solution; interviewers only check correctness.
State the O(n^2) brute force and its cost, note that n^2 ≈ 4 × 10^10 is too slow, and look for an O(n log n) or O(n) approach (sorting, hashing, two pointers, heap).
questions.explanation: Stating the brute force anchors correctness and shows reasoning. The constraint then tells you the target complexity: about 4 × 10^10 operations is far too many, so you need near-linear time. Backtracking is exponential and worse.
rationales: Changing the problem is not a solution.
Backtracking is for small n and exhaustive search.
Complexity matters and the brute force would time out.
Correct. Use the constraint to choose the target complexity.

questions.stem: Which statement about the class NP is correct?
options: NP contains decision problems whose yes-instances have certificates that can be verified in polynomial time; P is contained in NP.
NP and NP-complete are the same class.
A problem in NP always requires exponential time.
NP is the set of problems that cannot be solved in polynomial time.
questions.explanation: NP stands for nondeterministic polynomial time and is characterised by polynomial-time verification of certificates. Every problem solvable in polynomial time is also verifiable in polynomial time, so P ⊆ NP. Whether P = NP is open.
rationales: Correct.
NP-complete problems are the hardest problems in NP; NP also contains easy problems in P.
Problems in P are in NP and run in polynomial time.
This is the common 'non-polynomial' misreading.

questions.scenario: A team suspects their 'assign exams to time slots with no student clash' problem is NP-hard. One engineer writes a polynomial-time reduction that turns any exam-scheduling instance into a SAT formula.
questions.stem: What does this reduction establish?
options: Exam scheduling is NP-hard.
Exam scheduling is no harder than SAT (it is in NP), but not that it is NP-hard; for hardness, reduce a known NP-complete problem such as graph colouring to exam scheduling.
SAT can be solved in polynomial time.
P = NP.
questions.explanation: A reduction A ≤p B transfers algorithms from B to A and hardness from A to B. Reducing exam scheduling to SAT means a SAT solver can solve it, an upper bound. To prove hardness, reduce a known NP-complete problem to the new problem.
rationales: The direction is backwards for proving hardness.
Correct. Hardness flows from the known hard problem to the target.
Nothing about SAT's complexity changes.
No result about P versus NP follows.

questions.scenario: A logistics product needs exact optimal delivery routes visiting every stop once (a travelling salesman variant). Instances range from 8 to 2,000 stops.
questions.stem: Which two elements belong in a reasonable plan? (Select two.)
options: Sort stops by distance from the depot and visit them in that order, which is optimal.
Promise customers a polynomial-time exact algorithm after enough optimisation work.
Use exact search (branch and bound or bitmask DP) for small instances.
Use approximation algorithms or heuristics for large instances and report solution quality rather than claiming optimality.
questions.explanation: The decision version of TSP is NP-complete, so no polynomial exact algorithm is known. Exact exponential methods are practical for small instances, and approximation or heuristics handle large ones. A simple sort-by-distance greedy has no optimality guarantee.
rationales: This greedy rule can produce long zig-zag routes and is not optimal.
That would imply P = NP, which no one has shown.
Correct. Exponential search is fine when n is small.
Correct. This is the standard response to NP-hard optimisation at scale.
